sens: Aquatic plant with flexible, hollow stems that grows in wet and marshy areas
Rope or woven object made from the fibers of this plant
That which is weak, humble, or insignificant
That which collapses or bends under weight
Attitude of humility or submission, symbolized by bending
H0100.detail:
1. The reed is a common aquatic plant with soft, hollow stems; the Bible mentions it to refer to woven or twisted objects. In Job 40:21, the "reed" in the nostrils of Leviathan remains a mystery for translators — perhaps a shape or object, but mainly a symbol of the wildest and most untamed creature.
2. Its fibers were used to make flexible ropes, utensils, or "boilers" — vessels that can boil (Job 41:11), evoking the idea of something flexible, capable of containing, but also of transforming.
3. In the prophecies of Isaiah, the reed metaphorically represents the small, weak, and insignificant of Israel and Egypt, in contrast to the "palm branch" (the great, the powerful). In Isaiah 9:13 and 19:15, God will "pull up" the reed, symbolizing the elimination of the weak.
4. The reed, as a plant that naturally bends, becomes the image of bending and lowering. It is a passive, flexible, obedient posture.
5. In Isaiah 58:5, "bending the head like a reed" depicts the humility of fasting: the body that bends, inclines, submits — a posture of a humble heart before God.
H0100.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of flexibility and lowering. Its primary meaning refers to the actual plant, common in the marshes of the Near East; but it quickly shifts to the image of bending and weakness. The physical flexibility of the reed makes it a natural symbol of humility and non-resistance.
H0100.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always in a symbolic context rather than a botanical one. In the descriptions of Leviathan (Job 40:21 and 41:11), it retains a shade of concrete reality, even if obscure. In Isaiah, especially in prophetic context, it becomes a figure of the weak and despised: those who bend before the powerful, or those who are crushed. In Isaiah 58:5, the bent reed becomes the language of the body in authentic fasting — the physical expression of repentance and submission to God.
H0100.portee: The reed teaches that weakness and humility are not defects to be hated, but postures before God. God cares about the bent reed, the heart that humbles itself (Isaiah 58:5), far more than about pompous appearances. This image reminds us that true strength lies in flexibility, obedience, and the absence of proud rigidity — a lesson for the Christian seeking to bow before the Lord.

sens: Hollow container used to hold or pour liquids
Rounded shape, elegant curve of a part of the body
Set of descendants or members of a family
H0101.detail:
1. The basin is a hollow container, a cup used to hold or manipulate liquids, especially in religious rites: in Exodus 24:6, Moses puts the blood of the sacrifice in it for the sprinkling of the altar.
2. By its hollow and rounded aspect, the word also designates the elegant curves of the human body, particularly the chest: in Song of Solomon 7:3, the well-formed chest of the beloved is compared to a basin containing fragrant wine, an image of a harmonious and attractive shape.
3. By metaphorical extension, the basin signifies the entire set of descendants or dependents of a household, its "offspring": in Isaiah 22:24, the house of his father extends like a basin overflowing with its numerous descendants, small or large.
H0101.origine: The Hebrew word aggan comes from a root evoking a hollow, rounded, or bulging shape. Its basic image is that of a hollow, a cavity capable of holding. In Greek, this word is rendered by the term liknis or by words designating vessels and containers. The family of Hebrew words around this root explores the idea of rounded, concave, or overflowing shapes.
H0101.emploi: This word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. It first designates a concrete utensil of worship: the basin that receives the blood of sacrifices during the Sinai ceremony (Exodus 24:6). It is then used in the love poetry of the Song of Solomon to evoke physical beauty, the graceful roundness of a chest (7:3). Finally, it takes a fixed, almost metaphorical meaning to designate the abundant descendants of a household (Isaiah 22:24), where the basin becomes the image of a family overflowing with many offspring. The word thus shifts from the concrete to the sensitive, then to the figurative.
H0101.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible does not hesitate to describe the human body with respect and poetry, celebrating its beauty. It also shows how a simple word, that of a worship container, enriches the poetic and symbolic language of faith: the utensils of the sanctuary become images of the beloved body and of divine blessing in descendants.

sens: Group of soldiers forming a military unit
Division of an army, detachment
Body of warriors grouped for a common action
Multitude of armed people or in movement
H0102.detail:
1. A troop is an organized group of soldiers who fight together under the same command. In Ezekiel 38:9, the prophet sees Gog attacking "like a storm" with "all your troops," meaning all of his coordinated military forces.
2. The word also designates a division or section of a larger army, an autonomous detachment. When Ezekiel 17:21 speaks of the "fugitives from all his troops" who fall by the sword, it evokes the scattered remnants of combat groups that have been defeated.
3. More broadly, a troop is any grouping of warriors or fighters acting together, even without a strict military structure. In Ezekiel 38:22, God's judgments fall upon Gog "and upon his troops, and upon the many peoples who will be with him": this is the entire mass of assembled warriors.
4. The word can also evoke a multitude in motion, a large crowd of armed people or those ready for battle, particularly in a context of invasion or military mobilization.
H0102.origine: The Hebrew word אֲגַף (agaph) probably comes from a root meaning the action of gathering or grouping. The fundamental meaning is that of a "wing" or a "formation" — like the wing of an army on the battlefield. In the Greek Bible (Septuagint), this word is often rendered by a term meaning "side" or "part" of an army. The image is that of warriors gathering and tightening to form a compact and mobile force.
H0102.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in the prophet Ezekiel, in chapters 12, 17, and 38-39. It always designates military forces in a context of divine judgment upon the nations. Ezekiel uses it to speak of the army of King Zedekiah that is scattered (12:14, 17:21), and then especially of the immense coalition of Gog that invades Israel (38:6, 38:9, 38:22, 39:4). In all these cases, the "troop" is a group of warriors that will either be scattered or destroyed by the judgment of the Lord. The word reinforces the idea of an organized force standing against God and His people.
H0102.portee: This word reminds the reader that God rules over all military powers, no matter how organized and numerous they may be. Even the most formidable troops, assembled in great numbers, cannot withstand divine judgment. For the believer, it is an assurance that no one, no human or enemy force, can annihilate the people of God without facing the Lord Himself.

sens: to gather and pile up things in large quantities
to accumulate provisions or resources for future days
to gather the fruits of a harvest
H0103.detail:
1. Amasser means to gather and pile up: it is the action of putting together a large quantity of something. It is concrete: one stacks, one accumulates (Proverbs 6:8: the ant "gathers" during the harvest, meaning it collects and stores grain).
2. The word especially evokes the accumulation of provisions for the future: one gathers to have something to eat later, one prepares a reserve (Proverbs 10:5: "He who gathers in summer is a wise son," he thinks of winter).
3. In the agricultural context, to gather means to harvest and collect: it is the fruit of labor in the fields (Deuteronomy 28:39: you will not make a "harvest" — literally, you will not gather — because the locusts will eat your vines).
H0103.origine: The Hebrew root agar evokes the action of gathering in heaps. It belongs to the family of words related to accumulation and collection. The verb is commonly used to describe the harvest and storage of goods, particularly in wisdom texts that focus on the prudent management of resources.
H0103.emploi: The verb appears 3 times in the Hebrew Bible, all usages provided. It is characteristic of the vocabulary of harvest and foresight: in Deuteronomy 28:39, in a blessing and curse, it describes what the farmer will not be able to do if God curses him; in Proverbs 6:8 and 10:5, it illustrates the wisdom of one who works in summer to anticipate winter or a bad season. It is a practical word, rooted in agricultural life and the morality of the Old Testament.
H0103.portee: Gathering teaches that foresight is not a fault but a virtue. The wise person accumulates, prepares, thinks of tomorrow — this is what distinguishes him from one who sleeps or wastes. But the word also reminds us that every harvest is a gift from God: one gathers only if God allows it, and the loss of harvest is His judgment.

sens: Written message intended to be sent to someone
Official or administrative document bearing an authority's decision
H0104.detail:
1. A letter is a written message sent over a distance to communicate with someone. It is the means of transmitting information, requests, or orders when one cannot speak in person. In Ezra 4:8, Rehum and Shimshai write a letter to King Artaxerxes to report problems concerning Jerusalem: it is an official written communication sent to a distant authority.
2. A letter can also refer to an official document bearing authority: a written statement signed by a person in a position of power, which becomes a sort of written decision or order. In Ezra 5:6, the copy of the letter sent to King Darius by Tattenai, the governor, is mentioned: it is an administrative document that carries authority and can be copied for archiving or record-keeping.
H0104.origine: The Aramaic word אִגְּרָא comes from the same root as the Hebrew אִגֶּרֶת (igguèreth), both derived from a basic image related to writing and transmission. It is a word specific to the later books of the Old Testament, notably Ezra, where Persian rule made the use of official written communications common. The Aramaic word reflects the historical context of these accounts: after the exile, the Judeans live under Persian administration and communicate with the authorities in writing.
H0104.emploi: The word appears only three times in Ezra (4:8, 4:11, 5:6), all usages concerning communications between Persian authorities and the government of Jerusalem. In Ezra 4:8-11, Rehum and Shimshai write a letter to King Artaxerxes to report that the Judeans are rebuilding the Temple, which disrupts the established order. In Ezra 5:6, it is Tattenai who sends a letter to King Darius. These three occurrences show that the word is strictly used for official documents of the Persian administration, never for private or personal correspondence. It is an administrative and political term.
H0104.portee: This word reminds the reader that the reconstruction of Jerusalem after the exile takes place under Persian oversight, through formal bureaucratic channels. The letters mentioned here show how opposition to God's plans goes through official procedures, and how God governs despite the political and administrative obstacles that earthly authorities place in the way of His people.

sens: Shallow, wide, and open container used to hold liquids or other materials
In a cultic context, sacred vessel of the Temple for ablutions or offerings
H0105.detail:
1. The basin is a widely open, shallow container made to hold water or other substances — the image is that of a flat, flared cup rather than a closed jug. In Ezra 1:9, Ezra lists the treasures of the restored Temple: among the gold and silver vessels offered for worship, the basins are mentioned alongside knives and other utensils, testifying to their ritual importance.
2. In the Temple of Jerusalem, the basin was a sacred object used for ritual ablutions (to purify with water) or to collect the blood of sacrifices. These vessels were made of gold or silver according to their rank in the worship, and were among the most precious goods of the sanctuary.
H0105.origine: The Aramaic word אֲגַרְטָל likely comes from an ancient Semitic root related to the idea of containing or carrying. The form suggests a borrowing from a neighboring language — perhaps Persian or a language of the ancient Levant — reflecting the cultural contacts of the Near East. This type of vessel was common in religious contexts throughout the Mediterranean and Near Eastern regions.
H0105.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezra 1:9, in the account of the return from exile and the reconstruction of the Temple. Ezra lists the sacred vessels that King Cyrus has released for the Jews to bring back to Jerusalem. This unique mention shows that the basin was an important object of Temple worship, worthy of being inventoried among the most precious treasures — the text counts dozens in gold and thousands in silver.
H0105.portee: This passage reminds us of the preciousness of the worship rendered to God and the symbolic value of each object in the sanctuary. The basins, like all these vessels, were not mere utensils: they embodied the separation between the sacred and the profane, and their restoration marked the renewal of communion with God after the exile. For the believer, this underscores that even the most humble objects of worship carry spiritual dignity.

sens: Closed hand, clenched fist
Blow delivered with the fist
Act of violence or aggression
H0106.detail:
1. The fist is the hand closed with the fingers folded: it is the natural form of the hand ready to strike. In Exodus 21:18, in the law concerning quarrels, the fist is mentioned as the instrument of a fight between two men — one strikes the other with a stone or with the fist, which can cause serious injuries.
2. The fist also refers to the blow itself, the action of striking: it is by extension the physical violence exercised with closed fists. This appears in the same verse from Exodus where the impact of the fist is a legal fact that the law weighs the consequences of.
3. Isaiah 58:4 uses the expression "striking wickedly with the fist" to describe a malicious aggression, not in honest rebellion but with the intent to harm. The prophet reproaches the Israelites for fasting insincerely: they dispute and quarrel violently instead of seeking justice and peace.
H0106.origine: The Hebrew word אֶגְרֹף (egrouph) comes from a root that evokes the idea of closing, of tightening. The fist is literally the hand tightened, closed into a ball. This word belongs to the concrete vocabulary of the body and physical strength, common in accounts of confrontation or justice.
H0106.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. It first appears in Exodus 21:18, in the covenant code, to define a type of blow during a quarrel — a legal case that the law must adjudicate. It reappears in Isaiah 58:4, where the prophet uses it to criticize false piety: fasting while fighting with the fist does not honor God. In both cases, the fist symbolizes a violent and brutal action, in rupture with the order or justice that God demands.
H0106.portee: The fist reminds us that physical violence has legal and moral consequences. In Exodus, the law even protects the one who fights: it does not ignore violence, it regulates it. In Isaiah, the prophet shows that an outward religion (fasting) that coexists with aggression towards others is a sham: God desires heart transformation, not the pious gestures of a violent person. It is a call to moral integrity and peace.

sens: written or message transmitted from one person to another
official document bearing authority (from the king, a leader)
written correspondence
H0107.detail:
1. A letter is a written message sent to someone to communicate information. Hezekiah "wrote letters" to invite Israel to celebrate Passover (2 Chronicles 30:1): an act of communication at a distance.
2. In a political or administrative context, the letter is primarily an official document endowed with authority. Nehemiah requests from the king "letters for the governors" (Nehemiah 2:7): these royal writings open doors and command obedience. It is an instrument of power.
3. The letter can also be a missive of threat or derision: Sanballat sends Nehemiah "an open letter" to intimidate him (Nehemiah 6:5). The word then designates any writing intended to influence or provoke a reaction from the recipient.
H0107.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of bending or folding (as one folds parchment or papyrus). The related Aramaic (igra) shows that this vocabulary was shared by the peoples of the Levant. In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates the corresponding Hebrew when the context speaks of official written communications.
H0107.emploi: This word appears 10 times, mainly in the later historical books (Nehemiah, Esther, 2 Chronicles). It almost always designates royal letters or those from high officials: Hezekiah summons Israel by letter (2 Chronicles 30:1, 30:6), Nehemiah obtains letters of passage from the Persian king (Nehemiah 2:7, 2:8, 2:9), Sanballat resorts to a letter to threaten (Nehemiah 6:5). In the book of Esther, the word reappears for the royal edicts concerning the Jews. Each time, the letter carries authority and compels obedience.
H0107.portee: This word reminds us that before electronics, writing was the only means to transmit authority at a distance and leave a trace. For the believer, this sheds light on how God also spoke through his servants and prophets: his word, like a royal letter, must be received and obeyed. It also highlights the importance of faithful communication in governance and collective life.

sens: Mist or cloud of moisture rising from the earth
Vapor or humidity that rises in fine suspension
H0108.detail: 1. The word designates a mist or a light cloud of moisture rising from the earth to water its surface: it is dew or water vapor in visible form. In Genesis 2:6, before God causes rain to fall, a vapor rises from the ground and moistens it — it is the natural irrigation mechanism that preserves vegetation. 2. The word also describes the process by which water transforms into fine invisible droplets that rise into the air to later form rain. In Job 36:27, God draws the drops of water and reduces them to vapor, demonstrating his dominion over the natural water cycle: it is an act of divine power.
H0108.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the idea of something humid and elusive that rises. The word belongs to a simple and observational lexical field: it is the vocabulary of the farmer who sees the morning mist or the cloud forming. It describes a visible and elemental phenomenon, fundamental for agricultural life in the Middle East.
H0108.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Genesis 2:6, it appears in the creation narrative: God creates a world where vapor rises from the earth to sustain life. In Job 36:27, the wise Elihu uses it to show how God governs the water cycle with wisdom and power. In both cases, it is a natural phenomenon but of which God is the author and master.
H0108.portee: This simple word reminds us that God does not merely create once: he maintains every day the vital mechanisms that sustain creation. The vapor that rises, the water that circulates, the rain that nourishes — all of this is the work of his wisdom. It invites the believer to see in the daily natural phenomena the hands of God at work.

sens: Cause pain, moral distress to someone
Experience deep sadness oneself
Afflict, overwhelm someone with grief
H0109.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the action of causing sorrow to someone, inflicting a heartache. This is what God does in speaking to Eli: he will allow one of his descendants to survive, but "sadden" his soul, meaning to make him experience deep sorrow at seeing the death of others (1 Samuel 2:33).
2. The word can also refer to the feeling of sadness experienced by the one who suffers this pain: to be moved, afflicted, morally downcast.
3. In its strongest usage, "sadden" means to ravage someone with pain, to consume them with grief to the point of completely overwhelming them.
H0109.origine: The Hebrew word אָדַב comes from a root that expresses the idea of deep pain and affliction. It is akin to the state of a person who is overwhelmed by sorrow, who loses their momentum and strength under the weight of despair. The verb is generally used in the causative form (Hiph): not merely to be sad, but to cause sadness in others.
H0109.emploi: The verb אָדַב appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 2:33, in God's judgment against Eli the priest. God announces that he will allow one of his descendants to live, but he "saddened" him by seeing him deprived of offspring and full of bitterness. Thus, it is a term reserved for a moment of serious divine judgment, expressing how God afflicts the one who has offended him. The unique usage underscores the dramatic weight of this judgment.
H0109.portee: This word reveals how God's judgment is not mere destruction: it can be a persistent affliction, a heartache inflicted on one who has disobeyed. For the believer, this shows that distance from God is a source of deep sadness, and that divine discipline touches the soul above all. It is also a reminder that God sees the heart and knows all its pains.

sens: son of Ishmael and grandson of Abraham
member of the genealogy of Arab peoples
H0110.detail:
1. Adbeel is one of the twelve sons of Ishmael, listed alongside his brothers such as Kedar, Nebajoth, and others (Genesis 25:13). He represents a branch of Abraham's descendants through his son Ishmael.
2. He embodies the genealogy of the Arab peoples of antiquity. The genealogical lists in the Bible trace the origins of the neighboring peoples of Israel and show how all human beings descend from a common root (1 Chronicles 1:29).
H0110.origine: The name Adbeel literally means "punished by God" or "God has punished" (from ad = punish and el = God in Hebrew). It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the divine name, which was common among ancient Arabs. The name expresses a relationship to God, although its exact historical context is unknown to us.
H0110.emploi: Adbeel appears twice in the Bible, always in genealogical lists: in Genesis 25:13 as the third son of Ishmael, and in 1 Chronicles 1:29 as a confirmation of this genealogy. These lists serve to establish the origins of the Arab peoples contemporary to the patriarchs. Adbeel is never mentioned individually in a narrative or specific event, but only as a link in the genealogical chain connecting Abraham to his distant descendants.

sens: Young Edomite prince who fled to Egypt
Enemy that God raised against Solomon
H0111.detail:
1. Hadad was a young prince of the kingdom of Edom who fled to Egypt with his father's servants to escape the rule of David and Solomon (1 Kings 11:17). There he found refuge and was welcomed by the Pharaoh, whose sister he would marry.
2. God used Hadad as an instrument of punishment against Solomon: after the king turned away from the Lord by marrying foreign women and worshiping their gods, Scripture tells us that God raised up Hadad as an adversary to remind Solomon of the cost of his unfaithfulness.
H0111.origine: The name Hadad means "I will move gently" or "I will love," according to an ancient Semitic etymology. This name was borne by several important figures in the ancient Near East, including gods of Syrian worship. Here, Hadad is a historical Edomite figure whose fate illustrates how God uses political events in the Middle East to judge the unfaithfulness of His people.
H0111.emploi: Hadad is mentioned only once by name in the provided text (1 Kings 11:17), but the account concerning him extends over several verses in chapter 11 of 1 Kings. He is a young boy at the time of his flight to Egypt. Solomon made him a formidable adversary who, once grown, harassed him during his reign. His story illustrates how God's punishments against His chosen people can take the form of rivals raised against unfaithful kings.
H0111.portee: The story of Hadad teaches the reader that God judges royal unfaithfulness and that there are no insignificant consequences in abandoning the covenant with the Lord. It also shows that even a fleeing child can become, years later, an instrument of divine correction.

sens: Israeli leader at the return from Babylonian exile
H0112.detail: Iddo is an Israeli leader mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time of the return of the exiles from Babylon. He lived in Casiphia, a location not otherwise identified, and was responsible for a community that included the Nethinim (temple servants). Ezra sent him to seek men to serve in the house of God in the rebuilt Jerusalem (Ezra 8:17).
H0112.origine: The name Iddo means "I will praise him" or "the one who is praised," formed from the Hebrew root expressing praise. It is a theophoric name, meaning it includes a relationship to God and expresses trust in His goodness.
H0112.emploi: Iddo is mentioned only once in the Old Testament, in Ezra 8:17. He appears during Ezra's mission to reconstitute the temple's workforce after the return from captivity. His role suggests that he was a man of influence and trust, capable of mobilizing the temple servants who remained in Mesopotamia and directing them to Jerusalem.

sens: One who commands, who has authority over others; master of a house or estate.
Husband, spouse in a marital relationship.
King, sovereign who reigns over a people.
God, the Lord of the universe and all creation.
Title of respect, form of politeness towards someone superior or important.
Figure of spiritual authority, such as a prophet or an angel.
H0113.detail:
1. The lord is primarily one who directs, who commands: a master of a house or one who manages a property, its affairs, and its servants. In Genesis 24, Abraham's servant constantly speaks of his master's role in his daily life (Genesis 24:12, 24:36).

2. The word designates the husband in the couple: the wife recognizes in him one who has authority. In Psalm 45:12, the queen honors the king as her lord.

3. A lord can be a king, a sovereign who reigns over a territory or a people (Deuteronomy 10:17 speaks of the Lord God, "who shows no partiality").

4. The word applies primarily to God Himself: the Lord of the entire universe, the one who has absolute authority (Joshua 5:14, where Joshua encounters the lord of the Lord's army).

5. It is also a formula of respect and politeness: it is used towards someone one honors or depends on, as Abraham towards the three visitors in Genesis 18:3.

6. Sometimes it designates a spiritual authority: a prophet, an angel, or any being recognized as superior, before whom one bows.
H0113.origine: The Hebrew word אָדוֹן comes from a root expressing strength and solidity. Its primary image is that of a firm, established person, capable of holding a position of authority. The family of the word includes various forms that reinforce the idea of command and mastery. In the Greek translations of the Old Testament (the Septuagint), this word is generally rendered by κύριος (kurios, "lord"), the same term found in the New Testament to designate Jesus as Lord.
H0113.emploi: The word lord appears about 285 times in the Old Testament. It is extremely frequent in the account of Joseph, where it qualifies Potiphar, Joseph's Egyptian master, or where Joseph himself is called lord by those who obey him (Genesis 39-40). It is omnipresent in the relationships between masters and servants (Exodus 21), between kings and subjects, and between husbands and wives (Exodus 21:4-5). Applied to God, it becomes "the Lord" par excellence, surpassing all other lords (Deuteronomy 10:17). Its meaning varies little: it is always one who has authority, but the relationship changes according to the context — servant to an earthly master, creature to God, or wife to her husband.
H0113.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on authority and submission. For a believer, recognizing God as Lord means bowing before His will and absolute command. But it also reminds us that lordship carries a responsibility: a good lord, like God, cares for those under His authority. It is a key word for understanding how the Bible envisions the relationship between the Creator and His creation, and between human beings in their relationships of authority and service.

sens: Place of origin for families of Israelites returning from exile
H0114.detail: 1. Kerub-Addon is a place mentioned only once in the Bible, at the return from the Babylonian exile. It is a location from which certain families come back to Israel but whose descendants cannot prove their Israelite genealogy — a serious issue, since belonging to Israel was transmitted through lineage. The name suggests a site in Mesopotamia, likely a center where Israelites or foreigners settled during the exile (Nehemiah 7:61).
H0114.origine: The word "Addon" means "mighty" in Hebrew. It is a place name, probably a Babylonian or Mesopotamian site, also known as "Addan." The use of the double 'd' characterizes this proper name. The meaning "mighty" may evoke a place of some strategic or administrative importance in the Babylonian empire.
H0114.emploi: Kerub-Addon appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 7:61, in a genealogical list of exiles who returned under Zerubbabel. This list enumerates the families and places from which those who returned to Jerusalem after the Babylonian captivity came. Kerub-Addon is mentioned alongside other Mesopotamian locations (Thel-Melah, Thel-Harscha, Immer), all associated with families whose Israelite authenticity could not be verified by genealogical records.

sens: Fortified city of Judah, southwest of Hebron
H0115.detail: Adoraim is a city in southern Judah, located about 8 kilometers southwest of Hebron. King Rehoboam fortified it (2 Chronicles 11:9) in the aftermath of the schism that divided Solomon's kingdom, to defend his territory against external threats.
H0115.origine: The name literally means "double glory" in Hebrew (from "adar," which evokes splendor). This is the only place in the Bible where this name appears.
H0115.emploi: Adoraim appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 11:9, where it is listed among the cities that King Rehoboam fortified after the division of the unified kingdom (circa 930 B.C.). It is mentioned alongside Lachish and Azekah, other important fortresses in southern Judah.

sens: At this moment in the narrative, immediately after
After that, in the sequence of events
At that moment, at the same time
It is then that (marking a consequence)
H0116.detail:
1. "Then" marks the moment when the main action of the narrative occurs: it is the pivotal instant when things change. In Daniel 2:14, when the king orders the wise men to be killed, "then" Daniel rises to act — we move from danger to his response. It is the "at that moment" of the storyteller.
2. "Then" can also mean "after" in the logical sequence of events: one thing leads to another. In Ezra 4:23-24, after the king's decree, "then" the authorities cease the work and "then" the temple work stops — we see the chain of consequences.
3. Sometimes "then" simply designates the context of the action, without a marked break: "at that moment," "during that time." The meaning approaches a simple temporal indication.
4. "Then" can introduce a conclusion or a consequence: in Daniel 5:24, after the interpretation of the divine message, "then" the king acknowledges the supernatural power — the action logically follows what precedes it.
H0116.origine: It is an Aramaic word, the language spoken by the Jews in exile in Babylon. It comes from the Aramaic root related to the Hebrew "az" (H0227A), which also means "then." This word belongs to the same family as the concept of moment, the passage of time, the instant when things come together. It is a storyteller's word: it structures the narrative by marking the steps.
H0116.emploi: This word appears 53 times in the Bible, concentrated in the two books in Aramaic: Ezra and Daniel. It is the vital link that weaves the narrative, especially in Daniel where it appears more than 35 times. It structures the visions, the king's orders, the reactions of men. In Daniel 2, it accompanies each step of the dream story: "Then Daniel said," "Then the king embraced Daniel." In Daniel 3, it marks critical moments: "Then Nebuchadnezzar, enraged, gave the order." In Daniel 6, it punctuates Daniel's persecution step by step. The word is a true engine of the narrative.
H0116.portee: This small word reminds us that in biblical history, God acts in concrete time, at specific moments. "Then" teaches us to recognize turning points: the moment when God answers prayer, when He saves, when He judges. It invites us to remain vigilant, attentive to the "thens" of our own lives, the moments when God intervenes.

sens: One who possesses great strength, authority, or majesty
Of impressive magnitude, depth, or magnificence (referring to nature)
Of imposing grandeur (referring to trees or vegetation)
One who exercises power, command: chief, noble, dignitary
H0117.detail:
1. The word primarily describes power and majesty, particularly in the realm of authority and power. Psalm 136:18 speaks of "mighty kings" that the Lord killed, and Jeremiah 30:21 celebrates one "whose birth comes from him," a chief clothed in fearsome power. The word can also qualify the majestic greatness of God or His work: Psalm 8:10 exclaims, "How majestic is Your name in all the earth!"
2. For waters and nature, the word evokes imposing immensity. Exodus 15:10 speaks of the "depth" of the sea waters, where enemies sank like lead — an image of untamable power. Psalm 93:4 describes "the mighty waves" that lift their voice.
3. Majestically grand trees also receive this qualification. Ezekiel 17:23 describes a "magnificent" cedar planted on a high mountain, so imposing that all the birds find refuge there. The tree symbolizes here a power that dominates all creation.
4. As a noun, the word designates the "mighty ones," those who hold power: chiefs, nobles, dignitaries. Jeremiah 25:34 calls out to the "leaders" of flocks (the shepherds who govern), and 2 Chronicles 23:20 mentions the "considered men" who had authority.
H0117.origine: The Hebrew root expresses the idea of "power" and "impressive strength." The word refers to a presence or reality that commands respect through its magnitude or authority. Words of the same family denote greatness, majesty, and sometimes the fear they inspire. The term applies both to nature (great rivers, vast waters) and to powerful human beings or manifestations of divinity.
H0117.emploi: The word appears about 25 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, especially in the Psalms, the prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Isaiah), and historical narratives. It qualifies both people (kings, chiefs, nobles: Judges 5:13, Jeremiah 25:34) and impressive natural realities (rivers, waters, trees: Exodus 15:10, Ezekiel 17:23), as well as divine greatness (Psalm 8:10). When referring to a person, it emphasizes their authority and prestige; when describing nature, it highlights magnitude and majesty. Some rare uses bring it close to "leader" or "chief" (Jeremiah 25:34, 2 Chronicles 23:20).
H0117.portee: This word reminds us that true power is never trivial or ordinary — it inspires reverence. For believers, recognizing that God alone is truly "mighty" and magnificent (Psalm 8:10) directs the heart toward worship and surrender. The mention of the "mighty kings" defeated by God (Psalm 136:18) assures that even what seems invincible in human eyes does not escape divine sovereignty.

sens: Son of Haman, executed by the Jews during the vengeance of Purim
H0118.detail: Adalia is one of the ten sons of Haman, the sworn enemy of the Jews under King Ahasuerus. When Haman's plot is thwarted and Queen Esther obtains permission from the king to defend herself, the Jews rise up and kill their enemies, including all the sons of Haman. Adalia is listed among them in Esther 9:8, where his name is mentioned between Poratha and Aridatha. He thus represents the complete destruction of Haman's house and the fulfillment of divine justice in favor of the Jewish people.
H0118.origine: The name means "I will be lifted up by the Lord" (according to ancient sources), although its Hebrew structure is uncommon. It belongs to the list of names of Haman's sons, several of whom bear names of Persian or composite origin. This name appears only once in the entire Bible.
H0118.emploi: Adalia appears only once in the Bible, in Esther 9:8, where he is listed among the ten sons of Haman. It is a simple name in a list, with no action or words attributed to this character. His sole mention defines him only by his lineage (son of Haman) and by his fate (execution).

sens: To give a red color to a fabric, skin, or object
To be red or reddish in color
To present a bright, vivid red hue
H0119.detail:
1. To dye red means to color a textile or animal material with a red hue, through a dyeing or treatment process. It is a deliberate action: in the usages in Exodus, the skins of rams intended to cover the tabernacle are dyed red, making them durable and distinctive for the coverings of the Tent of Meeting (Exodus 25:5).
2. To be dyed or colored red means to have a red hue as a visible property. It is the state resulting from the previous action: a "dyed red" skin remains red (Exodus 26:14).
3. To shine or glow red applies to what has a bright and vivid red hue, often associated with nobility or beauty. In Lamentations 4:7, the text mentions that the Nazarites once had a ruddy glow compared to rubies, suggesting remarkable splendor and vigor.
H0119.origine: The verb אָדֹם (adam) comes from an ancient Semitic root meaning "to blush" or "to be red." It is related to the noun אָדָם (adam, "man"), whose traditional etymology links it to the redness of human skin or the red earth from which man was formed. The root expresses the idea of hue, of visible color that strikes the eye.
H0119.emploi: The verb appears about 10 times in the Old Testament, primarily in Exodus where it describes the ritual dyeing of ram skins for the tabernacle. The Segond translates it as "dyed red" or "red." Beyond dyeing usages, it is found in biblical poetry: in Isaiah 1:18, God speaks of red sins like scarlet that will be made white; in Lamentations 4:7, it refers to the red hue of the Nazarites of Judah, symbolizing their health and nobility; in Nahum 2:4, the text mentions the redness (probably of chariots or weapons). The word slightly shifts context: from practical dyeing to poetic or symbolic imagery.
H0119.portee: This word reminds us that God cares about the details of worship and the beauty of creation — including colors and art. For the believer, the red-dyed skins of the tabernacle symbolize holiness made concrete. The poetic usages (red sins, beauty of the Nazarites) show that the color red in the Bible carries meanings: guilt, vigor, nobility. It is a call to meditate on the visibility of our moral and spiritual state.

sens: A human being, male or female, created in the image of God
All humanity, the human species
A particular man, an individual among others
Each person, any human being
H0120G.detail:
1. The word primarily designates any human being considered in his individuality: "God said: Let us make man in our image" (Genesis 1:26) — it is the singular creature that God created, capable of consciousness and relationship with Him.
2. It also designates humanity as a whole, the human race: "There is no happiness for man except to eat and drink" (Ecclesiastes 2:24) speaks of the human condition in general.
3. It can mark a specific person in context: "Son of man, set your face" (Ezekiel 25:2) — Ezekiel is addressed as one of the men among others.
4. It also expresses universality: "No man shall dwell there" (Jeremiah 49:33) — it excludes every human being without exception.
H0120G.origine: The Hebrew word אָדָם (adam) probably comes from a root meaning "to be red" or "to be of red color" — a reference to the red earth (אֲדָמָה, adamah) from which God formed man according to Genesis 2:7. Man is thus the being created from dust, marked by his fragility and his link to the earth. The proper name Adam designates the first human, the one who "sets the tone" for all humanity.
H0120G.emploi: This word is one of the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible (over 500 occurrences). It appears massively in Genesis to speak of creation (Genesis 1:26-27, 2:5 and following), and then throughout the Old Testament in very varied contexts: the guilt of man before God (Genesis 6:5-7), the value of human life (Leviticus 24:17), the laws and prescriptions concerning "man" (Deuteronomy 8:3). The prophet Ezekiel is regularly called "son of man," presenting him as a mere human before the greatness of God. The word is used interchangeably for a particular individual or for all humanity.
H0120G.portee: This word reminds us that every human being — you, me, everyone — is created in the image of God (Genesis 1:27), and therefore bears an inviolable dignity. It also reminds us of our weakness: man is but dust and shadow (Ecclesiastes 2:24), entirely dependent on God for his life and well-being. This biblical realism about the human condition invites humility and trust in the One who created us.

sens: Human creature made in the image of God, created from the dust of the earth
Person of male sex, as opposed to woman
Human race, humanity as a whole
Each, any human being
H0120H.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the human creature in its entirety: body and soul, formed by God from the earth and enlivened by His breath. It is man as created in the image and likeness of God, dependent on Him and responsible before Him. Genesis 2:7 clearly shows this: "The Lord God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and man became a living being."

2. The word can specifically refer to the male, in contrast to the female. At the time of creation, man receives the first responsibility and authority: he cultivates the garden, names the animals, and is alone at first before God creates for him a "helper suitable for him." Genesis 2:22 illustrates this distinction: "The Lord God made a woman from the rib he had taken out of the man."

3. The word can be used collectively to refer to humanity or the human race as a whole, which God created and cares for.

4. Used without an article, it can mean "a man," "someone," "each one": any representative of the human species.
H0120H.origine: The Hebrew word אָדָם comes from a root meaning "to be red" or "to be ruddy," in reference to the red earth or the color of human skin. It is closely related to the word "adamah" (אֲדָמָה), the earth, the soil — man is literally "one from the earth." This connection emphasizes the earthly origin of humanity and its dependence on the soil for sustenance. The word has a universal scope in the Old Testament, designating both Adam himself, the first man, and every human being after him.
H0120H.emploi: The word appears 18 times in the Hebrew Bible according to the provided usages, concentrated mainly in Genesis 2-4, at the heart of the creation narrative. It first appears in Genesis 2:7 where God forms man from the dust, and then throughout chapter 2 to recount how man receives a mission (to cultivate the garden), a prohibition (not to eat from the tree of knowledge), and companionship (the woman). In Genesis 3, after the fall, the same word describes man facing his responsibilities, choices, and consequences. The usage is therefore dominated by the context of creation and relationship with God, emphasizing what it means to be human in the divine plan.
H0120H.portee: This word reminds us that humanity is created by God Himself, made of earthly material but enlivened by His breath, bearing His mark. Understanding that we are "man" or "woman" means accepting our finitude and our responsibility: we are created for a mission (to cultivate, keep, name), placed under God's authority, and called to communion with Him and with our fellow beings. This word also sheds light on why man's sin has consequences: the being created in the image of God cannot ignore Him without paying the price.

sens: The first man created by God
Man as a human being or humanity
H0121G.detail:
1. Adam is the first man created by God before the flood, mentioned for the first time in Genesis 2:19. He was married to Eve and fathered several sons: Cain, Abel, and Seth. His name means "red" in Hebrew. The Genesis accounts present him as the ancestor of all humanity, living nine hundred thirty years (Genesis 5:5) and fathering many sons and daughters (Genesis 5:4).
2. The word Adam is also used more broadly to refer to man or humanity in general. In Genesis 2:19 and elsewhere, it can simply be translated as "man" or "humanity" to speak of the human condition created in the image of God (Genesis 5:1).
H0121G.origine: The name Adam comes from a Hebrew root meaning "red" or "reddish," likely alluding to the color of the earth or flesh. The word may also derive from a root denoting humanity in general. This is why Adam, the first man, bears the same name as humanity itself: he is its prototype and beginning.
H0121G.emploi: The word appears about eleven times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the Genesis narrative (chapters 2 to 5). It is found in genealogies that list his descendants and calculate his age: Genesis 5:1-5 details his life and that of his direct descendants. Adam is also mentioned in historical genealogies (1 Chronicles 1:1) to establish the continuity of the human lineage. Later passages like Hosea 6:7 and Job 31:33 mention him to evoke the transgression of the first man and the introduction of sin into the world.
H0121G.portee: Adam symbolizes all humanity in its original condition and in its fall. As the first created in the image of God and the first to transgress His command, Adam represents both the dignity of creation and the reality of human sin. Meditating on Adam helps the believer understand his spiritual heritage and the necessity of salvation in Christ, who is presented in the New Testament as the new Adam.

sens: City located in the Jordan Valley, in Transjordan
H0121H.detail: Adam is a locality in the territory of Israel, situated in the Jordan Valley. It is mentioned as a geographical landmark during the miraculous crossing of the river: its waters stopped and rose in a heap near Adam (Joshua 3:16), allowing the people of Israel to cross the Jordan on dry ground to Jericho.
H0121H.origine: The name Adam means "red" in Hebrew, a hue that may evoke the color of the earth or stone in the area. This city is attested in ancient texts as a strategic stopping point in the Jordan Valley.
H0121H.emploi: Adam appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 3:16, where it is identified as a city near Zarethan. It marks the point where the waters of the Jordan stop during the miraculous crossing to the promised land. This site served as a geographical landmark known to the Israelites at the time of Joshua.

sens: of red or reddish color
of scarlet or bright red hue
of reddish or rust color (for an animal)
H0122A.detail:
1. The word designates the color red in its shades: from blood red to reddish or ruddy. It is a visible and striking color. The Moabites see the waters turn red like blood (2 Kings 3:22), a dramatic image of blood or destruction.
2. Applied to what shines or catches the eye by its brightness, the color red takes on a connotation of liveliness and beauty. The beloved in the Song of Songs is described as reddish, both white and radiant (Song of Songs 5:10) — a resplendent beauty.
3. For animals — horses and cows — it is a distinctive mark, a simple and observable physical characteristic. The red heifer (Numbers 19:2) and the red horses (Zechariah 1:8) are identified by this natural color. It is also the color of the garments of the one who treads the winepress, marked by the red wine of judgment (Isaiah 63:2).
H0122A.origine: The Hebrew root אָדֹם (a-dom) expresses the idea of redness or reddish hue. It is related to the name Edom, which means "red" or "he who is red" — a reference to the land and its people. The word carries no moral value in itself: it is a simple description of color, observable in nature and on beings.
H0122A.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, mainly in prophetic and descriptive passages. It applies to concrete realities: animals (cows, horses), clothing, water, blood. In the visions of Zechariah (1:8 and 6:2), the red horses are elements of prophetic visions without the color itself carrying a particular theological message — it is simply a detail of the picture. In Isaiah 63:2, the red color of the garments symbolizes divine judgment, the crushing of grapes in the winepress. The word remains always descriptive and concrete, never abstract.
H0122A.portee: This simple color reminds us that God perceives and describes the realities of the physical world with attention to detail. It also invites us, in Isaiah 63, to understand that divine judgment is as real and visible as the wine crushed in the winepress. In prophetic visions, it is a detail that anchors the divine message in a tangible reality.

sens: reddish dish, culinary preparation of red color
spicy or flavorful food
H0122B.detail:
1. The roux is a dish of red or reddish color that Jacob prepared, probably a stew or porridge. Esau, returning hungry from hunting, asks Jacob for it and agrees to sell his birthright to eat it (Genesis 25:30). This word gives its name to Esau, who is called Edom, meaning "the Red."
2. More broadly, the roux refers to a prepared, flavorful, and substantial food — the kind of comforting food that a tired man deeply desires. Esau's insistence on demanding this roux (the word is repeated twice in the verse) shows that this food powerfully attracts him, to the point that he sacrifices his inheritance to satisfy it.
H0122B.origine: The Hebrew word אֱדֹם (edom) comes from a root meaning "to be red" or "to blush." It describes both the characteristic color of a culinary preparation and, by extension, gives a nickname to Esau: his descendants will form the nation of Edom, whose name retains this same root. The word evokes the concrete image of reddish food that catches the eye and appetite.
H0122B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible in Genesis 25:30, where it designates the dish that Jacob cooks and that Esau covets. It is a very concrete and culinary term, recalling a simple but consequential domestic scene: this ordinary meal becomes the turning point of a family story. The context shows that the roux was appealing enough for Esau to renounce his birthright, revealing his lack of regard for his spiritual heritage.
H0122B.portee: This scene teaches how immediate and carnal desires can lead us to abandon our true riches. Esau sacrifices an invaluable asset — the birthright, linked to the divine promise — to satisfy a fleeting need. The roux becomes the concrete symbol of everything that distracts us from what truly matters, reminding us to remain vigilant against the temptations of the present moment.

sens: mountainous region to the south and southeast of Palestine, beyond the Dead Sea
people who inhabited this region, descendants of Esau
political and military power rivaling Israel
H0123G.detail:
1. Edom is primarily a land, a mountainous region (also called the land of Seir) located to the south and southeast of Palestine, beyond the Dead Sea. It is a rugged and arid terrain, bordering the kingdom of Judah. When Jacob receives a new name (Israel), his brother Esau becomes the ancestor of the people of Edom (Genesis 36:9).
2. Edom also refers to the people who inhabited this region: the descendants of Esau, called the Edomites. They formed a distinct people, with their own kings and cities (Genesis 36:31-43).
3. Politically, Edom is a power that Israel must confront or control. David conquers the land (1 Kings 11:15), but Edom revolts several times against Judah (2 Kings 8:20-22). It is a constant rival, sometimes a vassal, sometimes independent.
H0123G.origine: The name Edom means "red" in Hebrew, recalling either the reddish color of the lands of this region or the incident where Esau sells his birthright for a bowl of red lentils (Genesis 25:30). The people bear the name of their ancestor Esau, who himself received the nickname Edom. This genealogical origin is fundamental: the Edomites are cousins of the Israelites, both children of Isaac.
H0123G.emploi: Edom appears about 86 times in the Bible, mainly in the historical books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles) and prophetic books (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel). The word designates sometimes the territory, sometimes the people, sometimes the political kingdom. In the times of David and Solomon, Edom is conquered and subjected to Israel (2 Samuel 8:14). But it revolts several times, particularly during the time of Joram and Joash (2 Kings 8:20-22; 2 Kings 14:7). The prophets pronounce judgments against Edom for its hostility toward Judah, especially during the fall of Jerusalem (Psalms 137:7; Lamentations 4:21; Ezekiel 25:12-14).
H0123G.portee: Edom symbolizes in the Bible hostility toward the people of God and carnal pride. Although Edomites and Israelites are cousins by blood, they remain rivals; this tension reminds us that carnal proximity is not enough to create spiritual unity. The judgments against Edom teach that malice toward the people of God does not escape His justice, and that proud arrogance will ultimately be humbled.

sens: Nickname for Esau, meaning "the Red"
Descendants of Esau, Idumean inhabitants
Mountainous region in the southeast of Palestine
H0123H.detail:
1. Edom is the nickname given to Esau after his birth because he was red (Genesis 25:30). This nickname comes from the Hebrew word meaning "red," evoking the color of his skin and hair. The text recounts that Jacob calls him this when he offers him a meal in exchange for his birthright.
2. Edom also refers to the descendants of Esau, called Edomites or Idumeans (Genesis 36:1, 36:19). These generations bear the name of their ancestor and form a distinct nation with their own tribal leaders (1 Chronicles 1:51).
3. The word finally applies to the territory that these descendants inhabit: the mountainous region of Seir in the south and southeast of Palestine (Genesis 36:8, 36:21). This mountainous land, also called Idumea, becomes the homeland of the Edomites.
H0123H.origine: The name Edom comes from the Hebrew meaning literally "red." It is directly related to the physical color of Esau at his birth. The term expresses not only a personal characteristic but also family identity: all the descendants of Esau will bear this name, just as Israel becomes the name of Jacob and his children. It is a common biblical example of a name given according to a remarkable circumstance.
H0123H.emploi: Edom appears seven times in the provided texts, mainly in Genesis where it explains the nickname of Esau (Genesis 25:30) and outlines his genealogy (Genesis 36). The word gradually changes in meaning: first it is the personal nickname of the patriarch (Genesis 25:30), then it becomes the collective name of his descendants and their leaders (Genesis 36:19, 1 Chronicles 1:51), and finally it is also the name of the territory they occupy, the mountain of Seir (Genesis 36:8, 36:21). The different usages show how an individual nickname gradually becomes the name of a nation and its region.
H0123H.portee: Edom reminds the reader that biblical names often carry a deep meaning related to a circumstance or divine characteristic. The story of Esau and his nickname invites reflection on the value we place on things: Esau sold his birthright for a simple meal. It is also an example of how God creates distinct nations with their own histories, in the design of His salvation.

sens: Precious stone of red or reddish-brown color
Valuable stone used in ornamentation and luxury
H0124.detail:
1. The sardius is a precious stone of red or reddish-brown hue, deriving its name from its color. It appears in the description of the high priest's breastplate in Israel (Exodus 28:17), where it holds the first place among the twelve stones listed, highlighting its importance and remarkable beauty.

2. This stone symbolizes divine wealth and splendor. It is included in the list of stones that adorned the king of Tyre before his fall (Ezekiel 28:13), where it represents supreme magnificence and luxury, alongside gold and other rare gems.
H0124.origine: The Hebrew word אֹדֶם (odem) comes from the root עדם (adham), which evokes the redness and dark color of blood. This etymology directly links the name of the stone to its characteristic hue: red or reddish-brown. The word expresses the idea of something that is brilliant and precious due to its intense color.
H0124.emploi: The sardius appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in contexts of great solemnity. It is first mentioned in the breastplate of the high priest (Exodus 28:17 and 39:10), as the first stone of the four rows that adorned this liturgical garment. It reappears in the poem about the king of Tyre (Ezekiel 28:13), where it testifies to the lost splendor of a royal creature. In each occurrence, the sardius signifies excellence, worth, and exceptional beauty.
H0124.portee: The sardius reminds the believer that God delights in beauty and order, and that He has endowed precious stones with a splendor meant to reveal something of His magnificence. For the people of Israel, seeing this stone on the priest's breastplate was an invitation to contemplate the glory of God reflected in creation. It also warns us that material wealth and brilliance, if not refocused on God, become instruments of pride and ruin, as illustrated by the fate of the king of Tyre.

sens: Of pale or tender red color, leaning towards white
Presenting a hue between white and red
H0125.detail:
1. The word describes an intermediate color, neither distinctly red nor completely white — a particular shade that mixes white with a slight redness. This is the appearance that a wound or stain takes when it begins to inflame or when it is healing. In Leviticus 13:19 and 13:24, the priest examines wounds or burns that have this reddish appearance to diagnose leprosy.
2. The word can also apply to other surfaces: it is encountered to describe stains on clothing or walls of a house (Leviticus 13:49 and 14:37). In all cases, it refers to a coloration that is out of the ordinary and requires the careful examination of the priest to identify possible contamination or disease.
H0125.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root that expresses redness or the color red. It is formed to express a muted nuance of this color — neither pure red nor white, but a mix of the two. This family of words in Hebrew is related to the idea of what is visible and what manifests visually.
H0125.emploi: The word appears six times, exclusively in the book of Leviticus, in chapters 13 and 14, which deal with the laws on leprosy and purification. These are technical and medical passages where the priest must distinguish the different forms and colors of skin lesions, burns, or stains on clothing and walls. The reddish hue is a symptom that must be closely examined: it may indicate a leprous sore (Leviticus 13:42-43), or simply an infection or burn in the process of healing. The context is always that of medical-religious diagnosis in Israelite worship.
H0125.portee: This word reminds us that the Law of Moses contained very concrete rules of hygiene and diagnosis, concerned with the physical health of the people. It also shows the rigor with which the priest had to examine symptoms — neither too strict nor too lenient — to distinguish the pure from the impure and protect the community.

sens: city in the valley of Siddim
Canaanite city destroyed by God
H0126.detail:
1. Admah is a city located in the valley of Siddim, in Canaan, mentioned alongside Sodom, Gomorrah, and Zeboiim (Genesis 10:19). It had a king and participated in military alliances (Genesis 14:2, 14:8).
2. Admah has become a symbol of total and irrevocable divine destruction. Deuteronomy compares its ruin to that of Sodom and Gomorrah: the Lord destroyed it in His anger, leaving behind a barren land where nothing grows (Deuteronomy 29:23). The prophet Hosea invokes it as an image of desolation: "Shall I treat you like Admah?" (Hosea 11:8), evoking a merciless judgment.
H0126.origine: The name means "red earth" in Hebrew, likely referring to the color of the soil in this region of Canaan. Admah was a Canaanite city in the Jordan Valley, a companion of Sodom in the biblical story of divine judgment on the wicked peoples.
H0126.emploi: Admah appears five times in the Bible, always alongside Sodom, Gomorrah, and Zeboiim. First listed among the Canaanite cities (Genesis 10:19) and the warring kingdoms of the valley of Siddim (Genesis 14:2, 14:8), it gradually becomes an emblem of divine punishment. Deuteronomy associates it with total destruction and God's judgment (Deuteronomy 29:23), while the prophet Hosea cites it to express extreme rigor: the Lord hesitates to treat Israel as He treated Admah, so terrible was the judgment on this city (Hosea 11:8).
H0126.portee: Admah reminds the believer that God judges sin with justice and firmness, but also that His mercy surpasses His judgment. When Hosea invokes Admah, he shows that God hesitates to destroy Israel as He did these cursed cities: it is a call to repentance and an assurance that the heart of the Lord always leans toward compassion.

sens: The substance of the soil, what is cultivated and nourishes
A plot, a field, a piece of land
The visible surface of the earth, the material world
A territory, a country, a region
The entirety of the inhabited world
H0127G.detail:
1. The earth primarily refers to the material of the soil: the physical substance from which food is derived. In Genesis 2:7, the Lord forms man "from the dust of the earth" — a vivid image of our connection to this living matter. In Deuteronomy 28:4, "the fruit of your soil" speaks of the harvests that the earth provides to the farmer who cultivates it.

2. The word also refers to a plot, a specific field that one owns. In Genesis 47:19-20, the Egyptians sell to Pharaoh "their lands" — estates, properties. It is a concrete, measurable asset that can be bought, sold, or bequeathed.

3. The earth also refers to the visible world, the surface of the globe where creatures live. In Genesis 1:25, God creates "the animals of the earth," and in Genesis 6:1, "men began to multiply on the earth."

4. The word designates a political territory: a country, a nation. In Ezekiel 33:24, we speak of the "land of Israel": it is the land of Canaan that God has given as an inheritance to His people.

5. Finally, "earth" can refer to the entirety of the inhabited world, the whole creation. In Deuteronomy 28:63, the Lord threatens to "scatter you over the whole earth" — all of humanity and the vast world.
H0127G.origine: The Hebrew word אֲדָמָה (adamah) is very close to the name Adam (אָדָם), which means "man." This proximity is not a coincidence: man comes from the earth (adamah), he is derived from it, and he will return to it. In Genesis 2:7, the text plays precisely on this link: Adam is formed from the dust of the adamah. This is why this word carries within itself the idea of a living matter, a source of life, from which all beings arise and to which all return.
H0127G.emploi: The word adamah appears 187 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Torah (the first five books) and in the historical books. It is used very concretely: at the beginning of Genesis, it refers to the soil that God creates and from which He brings forth animals and man. Then, when sin enters the world (Genesis 3), the earth is cursed: it will yield its riches only through the sweat of the farmer. In the prophets, the earth also becomes a religious and political issue: possessing the promised land is a divine blessing, losing it is a curse. In Deuteronomy, adamah is linked to the promise: obeying God means enjoying the land and its fruits for a long time; disobeying means losing it (28:63; 30:18-20). The word thus always retains its material grounding — the soil, the field, the harvest — but it gradually becomes laden with spiritual and political significance.
H0127G.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God has entrusted us with a material, concrete world to cultivate and respect. But it also shows that our connection to the earth is fragile: it depends on our obedience to God and His blessing. The earth is never truly ours — it remains God's gift, which He can take away as easily as He can give. This word thus invites both responsibility towards this world and humility before Him who is its true master.

sens: Firm ground or surface of the earth
Inhabited territory, country
Earthly substance used for building
H0127H.detail:
1. The soil is the surface of the firm ground, where vegetation grows and which people work. In 1 Kings 17:14, during the drought, God promises that flour will not be lacking until He sends rain "on the face of the soil" — it is the rain that must fertilize the dried earth so that it can produce again.
2. The soil also refers to a territory, a country inhabited by a people. Jonah uses this word to speak of his "country" (Jonah 4:2), the one he wanted to flee from when God called him to Nineveh — it is the land, the geographical space that belongs to a nation.
3. The soil is the very matter of the earth, the substance from which clay or mud is derived for building. It is the raw material that God used to form all things.
H0127H.origine: The Hebrew word adama comes from a root that evokes redness, the reddish color of fertile soil. It is related to the word adam (man), because in the Genesis account, man is formed from the adama — he is literally "earth," created from the dust of the soil. This kinship between soil and man recurs constantly in the Bible: we come from the earth and we will return to it.
H0127H.emploi: This word appears rarely in the provided usages, but each occurrence shows an important facet. In 1 Kings 17-18, during the drought caused by God's judgment, the soil is barren — it does not rain "on the soil." This is an image of judgment: when God withholds rain, the soil can produce nothing. In Jonah, the word refers to the national territory, the concrete framework of a people's life. Adama is thus used for both the physical and material dimension (the land we cultivate) and for the political and identity dimension (the country we inhabit).
H0127H.portee: Understanding this word reminds believers that the earth is not neutral: it is God's creation, and it depends on His blessing. The drought in 1 Kings illustrates how God controls the fertility of the soil — He can bless it or curse it according to His will. For Jonah, the word evokes a man's attachment to his country and the difficulty of accepting that God diverts him from his plans. The soil is thus the stage where God's judgments and graces are enacted towards humanity.

sens: The habitable surface of the globe, the physical world where humans live
A region, a territory, a particular country
The earth as substance, matter that is cultivated or built upon
A plot, a parcel of land belonging to someone
H0127I.detail:
1. The earth refers to the surface of the habitable world, the terrestrial globe as a whole. It is the space where God has placed humanity to populate and cultivate. When the Bible speaks of "all the peoples of the earth," it evokes all the inhabitants of this habitable surface (Genesis 12:3).

2. It can also refer to a territory or a particular country: a geographical region with its borders, its people, its history. This is the meaning when discussing the land of Israel or a nation (Deuteronomy 12:1).

3. The earth is also the raw material of the soil: what can be cultivated to produce food, or from which materials are extracted for construction. It is the concrete element that the farmer works and that nourishes him.

4. A plot or parcel: a limited portion of land that one owns, a field or real estate. This is what a family can inherit or what one can lose (1 Samuel 20:15).
H0127I.origine: The Hebrew word אֲדָמָה comes from a root that evokes the idea of cultivating and fertility. It is related to the word אָדָם ("Adam"), the first human, whose name literally means "one who comes from the earth" — for God formed Adam from the dust of the earth. This etymological link underscores the deep relationship between humanity and the earth: man is born of the earth and must cultivate it to live. The same notion is found in several passages that remind us that the earth is God's gift to the people He has chosen.
H0127I.emploi: This word appears 22 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the books of the Pentateuch (Genesis, Exodus, Deuteronomy), in the historical books (Samuel, Kings), and in the prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Zephaniah). It is used to designate the land promised to Abraham and his descendants (Genesis 12:3, Deuteronomy 7:6), the terrestrial surface as God's domain (Deuteronomy 4:10), or the human kingdoms that reign over it (Jeremiah 25:26). Its meaning varies: sometimes it refers to the earth as a physical substrate, sometimes as a territory, sometimes as an inhabited world. In contexts of divine judgment or blessing, "the earth" becomes the stage for God's action towards the peoples.
H0127I.portee: Understanding this word helps the believer grasp how the Bible views humanity's relationship to creation: the earth is not just a backdrop, but God's very gift to His creatures, and particularly the promise made to Abraham and his descendants. It also reminds us that humans are not detached from matter, but rooted in the earth and responsible for its cultivation. Finally, it sheds light on the biblical view of history: God reigns over all the earth and His judgment is exercised over all the kingdoms that inhabit it.

sens: City in the territory of Naphtali
H0128.detail: Adama is a city listed among the towns allocated to the tribe of Naphtali during the division of Canaan. It appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:36, where it is included among the cities that Joshua distributes to the descendants of Naphtali after the conquest of the land.
H0128.origine: The name Adama, in Hebrew אֲדָמָה, literally means "earth" or "soil" — it is the same word that refers to dry land in general in the Bible. Some cities receive descriptive names: this one perhaps evokes the fertile or remarkable nature of the region. The city was likely located in the northern part of Canaan, in the mountainous territory of Naphtali.
H0128.emploi: Adama is mentioned only once in the Scriptures: in Joshua 19:36, during the detailed account of the borders and cities of the territory allocated to Naphtali. It appears in a list of localities that structured the political and religious life of this northern tribe of Israel. Beyond this mention, no biblical event takes place there; it is a territorial landmark rather than a center of narrative action.

sens: Fortified locality of the tribe of Naphtali
Passage or fortified crossing in the northern region of Israel
H0129.detail:
1. Adami-Nékeb is a place associated with the tribe of Naphtali, mentioned only once as a landmark during the delineation of the territorial borders assigned to this tribe after the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 19:33). It is a geographical point that helps define the southern boundary of the Naphtali region.
2. The name literally means "man of Adar," suggesting a fortified place or a defended passage, likely a small fortress or checkpoint that marked access to the region of Naphtali.
H0129.origine: The name "Adami" comes from Hebrew and means "man" (from "adam"), while "Nékeb" means "passage" or "narrow way." Together, Adami-Nékeb designates a fortified passage or a key crossing point in the geography of Naphtali. This type of double name was common in Canaan to designate strategic locations.
H0129.emploi: Adami-Nékeb appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:33, in the list of cities and landmarks that mark the boundaries of the territory of the tribe of Naphtali. It is a locality of which the biblical context tells us nothing else, except that it was a recognized cartographic landmark at the time of the land division. No particular biblical event is associated with this place.

sens: Inhabitant or native of the kingdom of Edom
Member of the Edomite people, descendant of Esau
Enemy or adversary of Israel
H0130.detail:
1. An Edomite is a person from Edom, the kingdom located southeast of the Dead Sea, east of the Jordan River. The term simply designates one who comes from this land, just as one would say "an Egyptian" or "a Syrian." Doeg is the most well-known example: he is the Edomite in the service of King Saul who denounces David to the king (1 Samuel 22:9).
2. More broadly, an Edomite belongs to the people of Edom, which the Bible constantly reminds us descends from Esau, the twin brother of Jacob (Israel). The Edomites appear in history as a neighboring and rival people to Israel: in 2 Chronicles 28:17, they "struck Judah and carried away captives."
3. On a religious and political level, the term often carries a negative connotation: the Edomite represents the enemy or adversary. However, the law in Deuteronomy 23:7 imposes a limit: "You shall not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother," reminding us that Jacob and Esau were brothers and that the peoples remain connected by blood.
H0130.origine: The word comes from "Edom" (H0123), whose primary meaning is "red." Esau received this nickname because he sold his birthright to Jacob for a bowl of red lentils (Genesis 25:30). The Edomites are thus literally "the people of Edom," the descendants of Esau. The Hebrew root expresses belonging to a people or region, similar to the suffix -ite in English.
H0130.emploi: The term "Edomite" appears a dozen times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the historical books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles) and the law (Deuteronomy). It sometimes designates an individual: Hadad the Edomite is a prince of the royal house of Edom whom God raises up as an enemy to Solomon (1 Kings 11:14); Doeg the Edomite is Saul's servant who massacres the priests of Nob (1 Samuel 22:9, 22:22). It also designates groups: in 2 Chronicles 28:17, "the Edomites" wage war against Judah. The term can even be translated as "Syrian" in 2 Kings 16:6, reflecting a textual variant or scribe confusion.
H0130.portee: This entry reminds the reader that the Bible recognizes the Edomites as a distinct people, with their own history and rights. The commandment in Deuteronomy 23:7 — not to hate the Edomite despite historical hostility — teaches that even enemies are still creatures of God and brothers by kinship. This lesson of temperance towards ancient adversaries sheds light on the biblical vision of justice and mercy.

sens: mountain pass of Judea
geographical landmark
transition zone between regions
H0131.detail: Adummim is a pass or ascent located west of Gilgal, in Judea. It is a mountain pass that marks an important boundary or landmark in the delineation of the territory of Israel. In Joshua 15:7, this pass serves as a major reference point for defining the territory of Judah, helping to orient the reader in a precise description of the borders ("it went northward toward Gilgal, which is opposite the ascent of Adummim"). In Joshua 18:17, Adummim again plays a similar role in the delineation of the territory of Benjamin, indicating a well-known place that contemporary readers could identify on the ground ("which is opposite the ascent of Adummim").
H0131.origine: The name Adummim likely evokes the notion of redness or rudimentary hue (a Semitic root related to the color red), which could refer to the color of the rock or soil in this mountainous region. The name may also suggest the idea of a pacified or calm area ("quieted ones"), although this interpretation is less certain. It is a toponym (place name) specifically associated with the geography of Canaan and the territory of Israel.
H0131.emploi: Adummim appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, both times in the book of Joshua. The term designates a mountain pass located in Judea, serving as a crucial topographical landmark in the description of tribal borders. In Joshua 15:7, Adummim helps define the northeastern boundary of the territory of Judah. In Joshua 18:17, the same geographical passage is involved in the delineation of the territory of Benjamin. These two uses show that this place was a well-established and easily recognizable landmark, used to clarify the territorial outlines of the Israelite tribes during the distribution of lands after the conquest of Canaan.
H0131.portee: Adummim reminds us that God has given each tribe of Israel a specific and delineated territory, which manifests His order and faithfulness. For the Christian reader, this passage invites meditation on divine sovereignty in the fulfillment of the promises made to Abraham and his descendants. These detailed geographical descriptions highlight the importance that God attaches to justice and clarity in the distribution of goods: each tribe receives precisely what belongs to it.

sens: Having a red or reddish color, particularly hair or complexion
Blond or light-colored hair and complexion
H0132.detail:
1. The word primarily describes a red or reddish color, like that imagined for Esau at birth, completely covered in red hair (Genesis 25:25: "The first came out all red, like a hairy garment"). It is a striking appearance, notable at birth.
2. In other contexts, the word extends to a lighter and blond coloration, far from pure red. David and the young King David are both described as "fair," not strictly red-haired (1 Samuel 16:12; 1 Samuel 17:42). It then denotes a light, bright hue, which can include reddish-blond hair or simply bright blond — making these young men remarkable and handsome in the eyes of ancient Hebrews.
H0132.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes redness and brightness. It belongs to a group of Hebrew words related to bright and vivid colors. In the ancient Greek translation of the Bible, it is rendered by terms expressing both red and light blond, suggesting that the exact nuance mattered less than the contrast with darker or brown shades more common.
H0132.emploi: The word appears three times in the Old Testament, always to describe the physical appearance of a notable character. It first applies to Esau at his birth, who is distinguished by his distinctive red hair. It then qualifies David and his brothers — particularly David when he is a young shepherd anointed by Samuel — as having a beautiful light coloration.
