In all three cases, the remark emphasizes an appearance that strikes the observer and, in the biblical context, may be linked to beauty, youth, or a unique destiny.
H0132.portee: For the reader, these descriptions of skin or hair color anchor the narratives in a concrete and vivid reality. The remark that David is fair and handsome reinforces the irony of his selection by Samuel: the Lord looks at the heart, not at outward appearance, even if that may be beautiful. The distinctive color becomes a memorable trait that helps the reader see these ancient figures not as abstractions, but as real men.

sens: Prince of Persia under the reign of Ahasuerus
Counselor to the king who had access to his presence
H0133.detail:
1. Admatha is one of the seven princes of Persia and Media who served King Ahasuerus. These men formed an elite council who "saw the face of the king," meaning they had free access to him and participated in the decisions of the kingdom (Esther 1:14).
2. His name literally means "a testimony for them" in Hebrew, although the Bible reveals nothing particular about his personality or deeds — he is simply listed among the highest-ranking dignitaries of the kingdom.
H0133.origine: The name Admatha is composed of Hebrew words meaning "testimony" and "them." It is borne by this historical figure from the time of exile and return, mentioned only in the book of Esther to establish the political context of the Persian court.
H0133.emploi: Admatha appears only once in the Bible, in Esther 1:14, where he is cited among the seven highest-ranking princes of Persia during the reign of King Ahasuerus (Xerxes). His name is included in the list of counselors who held the highest rank in the kingdom and enjoyed the rare privilege of seeing the king face to face, testifying to their political importance at the royal court of Susa.

sens: Metal base or pedestal on which columns rest
Foot or support of an object
Foundation or stable base
H0134.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the metal base that supports the columns of the tabernacle. In Exodus 26:19, it speaks of "forty bases of silver" on which the boards of the sanctuary rested: these bases were like feet of columns, solid and stable, preventing the structure from sinking into the ground. The same word is used for the bronze bases of the courtyard (Exodus 27:11).
2. More broadly, it designates any base or pedestal that supports something else. In Exodus 36:36, silver bases are cast for the columns of the tabernacle, which constitute its support. It is a structural element, essential to stability.
3. Finally, the word evokes the idea of foundation or base: in Job 38:6, it speaks of the "foundations of the earth," an image of the foundations on which the earth itself rests and which give it stability.
H0134.origine: The Hebrew word אֶדֶן (eden) comes from a root that expresses the idea of strength and firmness. Its primary meaning is "that which holds, that which supports." This is why it designates stable and solid bases: that which does not move, that which bears weight. Biblical uses always show it as a static element, which supports, which ensures the stability of what rests upon it.
H0134.emploi: This word appears 39 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the description of the tabernacle and its courtyard (Exodus 26 to 40, and Numbers 3 and 4). It is concrete and technical: each board of the tabernacle has two tenons that fit into two metal bases (Exodus 26:19, 26:21, 26:25). The bases of the courtyard are bronze (Exodus 27:10 to 27:18). There is no variation in meaning in these uses: it is always a material support. A notable exception: Job 38:6 uses the word figuratively to speak of the "foundations of the earth," its cosmic foundations. Song of Solomon 5:15 speaks of the "bases" as an image of stability and nobility.
H0134.portee: For the believer, the bases of the tabernacle remind us that God builds His sanctuary on solid and lasting foundations: everything that comes from God is stable, well anchored, unchanging. It is a call to trust: what we build our lives upon with the Lord will not collapse. The image of the foundations of the earth in Job 38:6 emphasizes that only God guarantees the stability of the world and our existence.

sens: Place in Babylon from which exiles returned
H0135.detail: Addan is a location situated in Babylon. At the time of the return from exile, some Jews who resided there could not prove their genealogical descent (Ezra 2:59), which initially prevented them from fully participating in the worship of the rebuilt Temple.
H0135.origine: The name Addan means "strong" or "firm" in Hebrew. This Babylonian locality bears a name that evokes solidity and resilience. In the lists of exiles, it also appears in the form Addon, a variant of the same name.
H0135.emploi: Addan is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 2:59, in the midst of the list of exiles who returned from Babylon under Zerubbabel around 538 B.C. This passage enumerates the families and localities from which the repatriates came. Addan is listed among the Babylonian places from which some of the returnees came, although they could not justify their priestly lineage.

sens: Title of respect and reverence towards God
Designation of the God of Israel in place of the divine name YHVH
Call or invocation addressed to God in prayer
H0136.detail:
1. It is a title that expresses respect and obedience towards a supreme authority — in this case, God Himself. The word evokes a hierarchical relationship where the speaker acknowledges the absolute authority of the one they are addressing. Abram says "Lord God" while imploring a promise (Genesis 15:2), thus expressing both his respect and hope in God.
2. In Jewish tradition, this word replaces the divine name YHVH (the Eternal) out of reverence: the sacred name of God is not pronounced, rather one says "Lord." The Segond translation often translates this word as "Eternal" precisely because it designates the God of Israel, whose name revealed to Moses is YHVH. In Ezekiel, the prophet regularly speaks of "the Lord God" to announce divine words (Ezekiel 37:12).
3. It is also a means of personally addressing God in prayer: one invokes Him as a benevolent master whom one pleads with. The Psalms and the prayers of the Pentateuch multiply this call: "Lord, hear me," "Lord, have mercy" (Psalms 71:16, Psalms 86:3).
H0136.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "master" or "lord" — one who dominates or governs. The same root gives words for "mastery" or "dominion." In biblical Hebrew, it is first used for a human master (a feudal lord or a boss), but when applied to God, it becomes the supreme title of reverence. This practice of saying "Lord" instead of the divine name strengthened after the Babylonian exile and reflects an increasingly cautious piety towards the name of God.
H0136.emploi: The word appears 425 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the Psalms, the Prophets, and the Pentateuch. It is used in three ways: (1) alone, to directly invoke God ("Lord, hear my prayer" in Psalms 86:3); (2) accompanied by "the Eternal" to emphasize the revealed and eternal nature of God ("Lord God" in Ezekiel 37:12); (3) in prophetic formulas such as "Thus says the Lord God" to introduce a divine word. The word does not change much in meaning according to the context: it is always an affirmation of divine sovereignty and an expression of reverence.
H0136.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God is not an abstract force but a personal authority with whom one can enter into relationship through prayer. The title "Lord" invites both humility (recognizing that one is not the master of oneself) and trust (relying on a benevolent master). By saying "Lord," one confesses that God governs our life and deserves our obedience and worship.

sens: Canaanite king defeated by the Israelites during the conquest of Canaan
H0137.detail: 1. Adoni-Bezek is a Canaanite military leader who rules over the city of Bezek at the time when the tribes of Israel begin to conquer the promised land. During a confrontation at Bezek, the Israelites capture him, cut off the thumbs of his hands and feet in retaliation, and then bring him to Jerusalem where he dies.
H0137.origine: The name means "my lord is Bezek" or "lord of Bezek": "Adoni" (adonim in the plural) means "lord, master" and designates a royal title or a deity in the Canaanite world, while "Bezek" is the name of his city. It is a typical name of local Canaanite leaders of that time, reflecting the fragmented political structures of Canaan before Israelite domination.
H0137.emploi: Adoni-Bezek appears three times in the Book of Judges, only in chapter 1 (verses 5, 6, and 7). He represents one of the first organized Canaanite resistances against the Israelite invasion: the Israelites find him at Bezek, engage him in battle, defeat him, capture him, and judge him by inflicting a mutilation (cutting off the thumbs of his hands and feet), which was a terrible form of punishment at the time. His story marks the beginning of the conquests of the Israelite tribes in Canaan and illustrates the violence of the conflicts that characterized this period.

sens: Fourth son of King David, rival of Solomon for the throne of Israel
A Levite teacher sent by King Jehoshaphat
H0138G.detail:
1. Adonijah is the son of David and Haggith, born during the reign of King David. He became a claimant to the throne after David, even organizing a lavish feast with sacrificed animals to proclaim himself king, thinking that Solomon would not reign (1 Kings 1:9). However, David had chosen Solomon as his successor, and Solomon thwarted this rebellion.
2. Another Adonijah appears in the account of Jehoshaphat, where he was sent as a Levite to teach the Law to the inhabitants of the kingdom, showing that this name also carried men of piety in the service of worship and faith in Israel.
H0138G.origine: The name means "My Lord is Jehovah" (Adon = lord, master; Yah = short form of the divine name). It was a name borne by several characters in the history of Israel, expressing a religious conviction. Although bearing the same name, these men led very different destinies: one sought royalty through ambition, the other served God through teaching.
H0138G.emploi: Adonijah mainly appears in the story of David's succession at the turn of the 10th century B.C. The account in the First Book of Kings shows him particularly active during his attempted coup d'état (1 Kings 1:5-1 Kings 1:51), where he received the support of General Joab and Priest Abiathar, while other nobles of the kingdom (the prophet Nathan, Bathsheba the mother of Solomon) worked for Solomon. After his failure, he sought to negotiate with Bathsheba (1 Kings 2:13-1 Kings 2:24), but was ultimately executed on Solomon's orders. A parallel occurrence appears in 1 Chronicles 3:2 in the genealogical list of David's sons. It was also the name of a Levite during the time of Jehoshaphat.
H0138G.portee: The story of Adonijah teaches that human ambition, even supported by a strong political base (the army, the priesthood), does not prevail against God's purpose. It also shows that the father's will prevails over the son's claims, and that seeking to usurp what God grants to another leads to ruin. For the believer, this account reminds us that seeking by one's own strength what God has not given exposes one to judgment.

sens: Levite sent by King Jehoshaphat to teach the Law in the cities of Judah
H0138H.detail: Adonijah is a Levite, meaning a member of the tribe of Levi dedicated to the service of the temple and to the religious instruction of Israel. King Jehoshaphat sends him on a mission with other Levites and priests to travel through the cities of Judah and teach the Law of the Eternal to the people (2 Chronicles 17:8). This is an example of the religious reform led by this king: rather than allowing spiritual ignorance, he organizes a true campaign of public instruction in his kingdom.
H0138H.origine: The name Adonijah means "my Lord is the Eternal" (from Hebrew "Adon" = Lord and "Yah" = the Eternal). It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the divine name within it. The same name has been borne by other characters in the history of Israel, including a son of David who revolted against Solomon, but here it designates a Levite unrelated to this royal rivalry.
H0138H.emploi: Adonijah is mentioned only once in Scripture, in 2 Chronicles 17:8, where he is listed among the Levites sent by King Jehoshaphat (circa 873-849 B.C.) in his campaign to teach the Law. The Bible does not provide further details about his life or ministry, but his presence in this list shows that he was respected and competent enough to be chosen for this important mission of religious instruction. His role illustrates the central function of the Levites: not only to serve in the temple but also to be teachers and spiritual guides for the people.
H0138H.portee: This character reminds us that the teaching of God's Word has always been at the heart of Israel's life. Adonijah, whose name proclaims that "the Eternal is Lord," embodies the faithful transmission of the Law: it is not enough for leaders to know the divine will; they must teach it to ordinary people in their cities. He is a model of discreet service, recognized by the king as trustworthy for this vital task.

sens: A leader of the people who participated in the reforms of Nehemiah after the exile to Babylon
H0138I.detail: Adonijah is one of the leaders of Israel who affixed his seal to the solemn commitment made by the people to live according to God's Law. He appears in the list of signatories in Nehemiah 10:16, alongside Bigvai and Adin, during the ceremony of renewing the covenant after the return from exile.
H0138I.origine: The name Adonijah means "My Lord is Jehovah" or "Adonai is Yahweh," formed from two elements: Adon (lord, master) and Yah (short form of the divine name Yahweh). It is a theophoric name, meaning a name that incorporates the name of God, very common in biblical Israel to express trust in God or His sovereignty.
H0138I.emploi: The character named Adonijah in Nehemiah 10:16 is a leader of Israel at the time of the return from exile, distinct from other Adonijahs mentioned elsewhere in the Bible (the son of David who coveted the throne, the Levite sent by Jehoshaphat). This Adonijah is part of the group of notables who acknowledge the Law and solemnly commit to following it in the context of Nehemiah's reforms in Jerusalem. His inclusion among the signatories of the covenant shows his status as an influential figure of the restored people after the exile.
H0138I.portee: This character reminds us that the restoration of Israel after the exile did not happen by miracle alone, but through the personal and solemn commitment of its leaders and people to obey the Law. The name Adonijah, proclaiming that the Lord is Jehovah, invites every believer to recognize God's authority in their own life.

sens: Canaanite king of Jerusalem at the time of Israel's conquest
H0139.detail: Adoni-Zedek is the name of a Canaanite king who ruled over Jerusalem when Joshua was conquering the territory of Canaan. His name means "my Lord is righteous" in Hebrew, which was a common royal title in Canaanite cities, reflecting the role of judge and guarantor of justice expected of a king. When he learns that Joshua has conquered Ai and that Gibeon has made peace with Israel, he organizes an alliance with other Canaanite kings to fight Israel (Joshua 10:1-3), but he will be defeated and killed by Joshua's forces.
H0139.origine: The name Adoni-Zedek literally means "My Lord is righteous": "Adoni" means "my lord" or "my master," and "Zedek" means "justice" or "righteousness." This type of theophoric name (containing the name of a deity or an invocation) was typical among the Canaanite kings of Jerusalem and other cities in the Levant. It expressed that the king was invested with divine authority and responsible for justice.
H0139.emploi: Adoni-Zedek appears twice in the book of Joshua (Joshua 10:1 and 10:3), during the account of the southern campaign in Canaan. He is presented as the king of Jerusalem who, seeing Joshua's military successes, fears for his territory and summons four other Canaanite kings (those of Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon) to form a coalition against Israel. This was a key moment in the conquest, as this alliance of five Canaanite kings represented the greatest organized resistance against Joshua and the Israelites.
H0139.portee: The story of Adoni-Zedek illustrates how the Canaanite kingdoms attempted to resist the establishment of Israel in Canaan. It shows that despite their alliances and military strength, the Canaanite kings could not stop God's plan for His people. It is a reminder that Israel's victory came from God, not from military superiority.

sens: Leader of an Israelite family who led his descendants from the Babylonian exile to Jerusalem
H0140.detail: Adonikam is a clan leader among those who guided the return of the Israelites from captivity to Jerusalem after the destruction of the temple by Nebuchadnezzar. His name means "my Lord has risen," evoking the idea of restoration or rebirth. Genealogical lists mention him as the founder of a large household: in Ezra 2:13, his descendants number six hundred sixty-six; in Ezra 8:13, some of his sons—Eliphelet, Jeiel, and Schemaiah—are listed among those who made the journey back with Ezra; in Nehemiah 7:18, another list counts him among the leaders whose sons returned, with six hundred sixty-seven souls.
H0140.origine: The Hebrew name אֲדֹנִיקָם (Adonikam) is composed of "Adon" (lord, master) and "Qam" (has risen, has stood). This composition evokes an action of rectification or raising up, which was perfectly suited to a man who embodied the renewal of the people returning from exile. The parallel with other names of clan leaders from the same context shows that he was a person of rank and responsibility.
H0140.emploi: Adonikam appears three times in the accounts of the post-exilic restoration. In Ezra 2, during the first list of returnees under Zerubbabel, he is cited with a significant number of descendants. In Ezra 8, his sons appear again among those who accompanied Ezra on a later expedition. In Nehemiah 7, a parallel enumeration—likely an administrative duplicate—mentions him again with a slightly different count (six hundred sixty-seven instead of six hundred sixty-six). These repetitions show that his descendants were numerous and faithful to the reconstruction project.

sens: High-ranking officer under King Solomon
In charge of taxes and royal corvées
H0141.detail:
1. Adoniram was one of the chief officers of King Solomon, son of Abda. He held an important position at the royal court alongside other high officials such as the chief of the king's household (1 Kings 4:6).
2. He was specifically tasked with collecting the kingdom's taxes and supervising the corvée workers, that is, the laborers requisitioned for royal construction projects such as the building of the Temple and the palace (1 Kings 5:14). He coordinated the monthly rotation of these men to Lebanon to cut cedar wood.
H0141.origine: His name means "my Lord is exalted" in Hebrew. He is also referred to as "Adoram" (אֲדֹרָם) in other biblical passages, notably in 2 Chronicles 10:18 where he is called Hadoram. These name variations reflect different textual traditions for designating the same person.
H0141.emploi: Adoniram appears twice in the accounts of Solomon's reign. First, he is presented as the head of the kingdom's tax administration (1 Kings 4:6), then he is mentioned as responsible for organizing the corvées that supplied the grand royal projects, particularly the extraction of cedar wood in Lebanon (1 Kings 5:14). These two roles show that he held the functions of financial controller and chief of public works.

sens: To shine by its greatness, nobility, or brilliance
To be worthy of notice and admiration for its strength or holiness
To make something great and glorious
H0142.detail:
1. The word primarily evokes the idea of something that stands out due to its greatness and majesty — an imposing beauty that catches the eye. In the song of Exodus 15:11, it asks: "Who is like you, magnificent in holiness?" — this rhetorical question highlights God's incomparability.
2. By extension, it means deserving attention and admiration for its remarkable power. The right hand of the Lord "has signaled its strength" (Exodus 15:6): it has manifested itself in a brilliant way, crushing the enemy — an act so great that it cannot be overlooked.
3. Finally, the verb can also mean "to make magnificent," "to proclaim in a grand manner": the law that the Lord wants to proclaim for Israel is a law "great and magnificent" (Isaiah 42:21), meaning worthy of reverence and solemn proclamation.
H0142.origine: The Hebrew root רדא (radah) means "to be wide," "to be noble," evoking the idea of a natural breadth of view and dignity. The word belongs to the poetic vocabulary of the Bible and is mainly used in hymns and solemn passages where divine power is celebrated. It expresses not only a quality but a public manifestation of that greatness.
H0142.emploi: The verb appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in solemn and poetic contexts. In Exodus 15:6 and 15:11 — excerpts from the victory song sung after crossing the Red Sea — it denotes the brilliant manifestation of God's strength. In Isaiah 42:21, it qualifies the law that the Lord wants to proclaim with grandeur. In each case, the word emphasizes not only an intrinsic quality (greatness, holiness) but also its public and noteworthy manifestation.
H0142.portee: This word reminds the reader that God's greatness is not only internal: it bursts forth before all who have eyes to see. Every act of divine power, every solemn word deserves to be recognized and proclaimed. For the believer, it is an invitation not to overlook the signs of divine majesty in their life and in history.

sens: the twelfth month of the Jewish calendar, corresponding to March-April
H0143.detail: Adar is the last month of the Jewish religious year. In the book of Esther, it plays a decisive role: it is in the month of Adar that the lot (the pur) is cast to determine the day of the persecution of the Jews (Esther 3:7), and it is also the month when the Jews defend themselves and triumph over their enemies (Esther 9:1). The thirteenth day of Adar has become a memorable day in the history of the Jewish people.
H0143.origine: The name "Adar" means "glorious" or "magnificent." This month bears this name due to its important position in the Hebrew calendar. It is during Adar that the festival of Purim is celebrated, commemorating the deliverance of the Jews under Ahasuerus, an event described as glorious for the people of God.
H0143.emploi: Adar appears eight times in the Bible, exclusively in the book of Esther. The month is mentioned during the casting of lots that seals the fate of the Jews in the Persian empire (Esther 3:7, 3:13, and 8:12), and then during the events of the thirteenth to the fourteenth days of the month, when the Jews defend themselves against those seeking their destruction (Esther 9:1, 9:15, 9:17, 9:19, 9:21). These references show the historical importance of Adar in the preservation of the Jewish people.

sens: The twelfth month of the Hebrew calendar, corresponding to March-April in our calendar
H0144.detail: 1. Adar is the last month of the Jewish religious year, a spring period. It is a month rich in significance: it is during this month that Passover took place and that the major reconstruction works were accomplished. In Ezra 6:15, the rebuilt Temple was completed and consecrated on the 3rd of Adar, marking the restoration of divine worship after the exile.
H0144.origine: The Hebrew name אֲדָר (Adar) means "glorious," perhaps evoking the magnificence of spring or the splendor of the month. This word draws from ancient Near Eastern calendars, particularly the Babylonian system to which the Hebrews conformed after the exile. The month bears a name that reflects the religious and agricultural importance of this period of renewal.
H0144.emploi: The word Adar appears in the Hebrew Bible to designate the twelfth month of the Jewish calendar. It is mentioned during major events in Israel's history: the construction of the Temple by Zerubbabel is completed in Adar (Ezra 6:15), marking a decisive moment of national restoration. In the biblical writings after the exile, this month holds particular importance, especially in connection with the festival of Purim that takes place during it.

sens: A large and majestic cloak or cape
Splendor, magnificence, honor
H0145.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a large and imposing garment, a cloak or cape that broadly envelops the body — the image is that of a flowing robe that covers and protects. In Micah 2:8, we see travelers being stripped of their garments after a battle, these ample robes being taken from them: this is the most concrete sense.
2. By extension, the word takes on a figurative value: it denotes splendor, magnificence, glory — as if someone were wearing a princely adornment. In Zechariah 11:13, when God speaks of the "magnificent price" at which He was valued, He uses this word to evoke not a garment, but the dignity, the shining honor that should be accorded to Him. It is the image of visible and imposing greatness.
H0145.origine: The Hebrew word אֶדֶר (eder) comes from a root that evokes breadth, what is wide and majestic. The same root produces words related to power and greatness. The central image is that of something that extends, that is ample — first a garment that flows widely, then by metaphor everything that is great, magnificent, and commands respect by its brilliance.
H0145.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible. In Micah 2:8, it is used in the concrete sense: the mantle taken from the defeated, a sign of their dispossession. In Zechariah 11:13, it shifts to the figurative sense: the "magnificence" of the price offered to the shepherd (the thirty pieces of silver for which Jesus will be sold according to Matthew 26:15) — a pitifully low price, hence the divine irony. These two uses show how biblical Hebrew moves from the concrete (a garment) to the abstract (glory).
H0145.portee: This word reminds us that in Scripture, visible splendor — a garment, a treasure — can symbolize the true value of a person or their work. In Zechariah, the Lord is valued at a derisory price by His people, despite His infinite magnificence: it is a lesson in humility about how the world fails to recognize the true greatness of God.

sens: A city of Judah located near Edom, in the southern territory
H0146G.detail: Addar is a small fortified city in the desert region of southern Judah, mentioned as a landmark in the description of the borders of the territory allotted to the tribe of Judah. It is located on the route from Kadesh-Barnea westward toward Karkaa (Joshua 15:3). It is a geographical location that helps to precisely delineate the promised lands.
H0146G.origine: The name "Addar" literally means "very glorious" or "very splendid" in Hebrew. It derives from a root expressing brilliance and greatness. It is a place name that carries the idea of magnificence, even though this small border city was of modest importance.
H0146G.emploi: Addar appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:3. It is listed among the cities and landmarks that mark the southern boundary of the territory of Judah, between the Negev desert and the border of Edom. This passage is part of the account of the division of the lands after the conquest of Canaan, where each tribe receives its inheritance.

sens: Son of Bela, grandson of Benjamin
H0146H.detail: Addar is a man from the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned only once in the Bible as the son of Bela (1 Chronicles 8:3). He is part of the genealogy of the descendants of Benjamin, listed during the time of Egypt and the wilderness.
H0146H.origine: The name Addar means "extremely glorious" in Hebrew, formed from a root that evokes glory and splendor. Its meaning reflects the genealogical importance of this character in the Benjaminite lineage, although few details are provided about him.
H0146H.emploi: Addar appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:3, where he is listed in the genealogy of the sons of Bela, who is himself a son of Benjamin. He is mentioned alongside other notable descendants of the tribe of Benjamin, such as Gera and Abihud. His name is preserved in the genealogical records of Israel, marking his place in the continuity of God's people.

sens: Open space where grain is threshed to separate the grain from the chaff
Symbol of separation between the good and the bad, the useful and the useless
H0147.detail:
1. The threshing floor is the place, usually outdoors, where farmers threshed wheat and barley to separate the grains from the chaff. The light chaff would blow away in the wind while the heavier grain fell to the ground — which is why Daniel 2:35 compares the debris of the statue to the chaff that is seen blowing away from a threshing floor in summer.
2. For the prophets and biblical sages, the threshing floor illustrates divine sorting: the Lord separates the good from the bad like the grain from the chaff. It is a vivid image of judgment and discernment.
H0147.origine: The Hebrew word אִדַּר (iddar) simply refers to the flattened and beaten ground where threshing took place. It is a place of daily agricultural work in Israel and the Middle East, simple and unremarkable at first — but it has taken on a strong symbolic charge in prophetic speech.
H0147.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible: in Daniel 2:35, in the description of Nebuchadnezzar's dream and its interpretation by Daniel. The giant statue, struck by a stone, is reduced to dust "like the chaff that escapes from a threshing floor in summer." Daniel uses this familiar image to show that earthly kingdoms, no matter how powerful they seem, will be scattered and destroyed like chaff in the wind — while God's eternal kingdom will grow and fill the whole earth.
H0147.portee: This image of the threshing floor invites the reader to meditate on God's judgment: He sees everything, discerning the just from the unjust, the lasting from the ephemeral. It reassures the believer going through oppression: empires that seem unshakeable will crumble, while Christ's kingdom will endure forever. It is a call not to fear human power, but to trust in God.

sens: High-ranking magistrate in the Babylonian administration
Advisor or royal officer responsible for administering justice or giving counsel
H0148.detail:
1. The term refers to a high-ranking magistrate in the judicial hierarchy of the Babylonian kingdom. In Daniel 3:2-3, these "great" judges are summoned by King Nebuchadnezzar alongside the satraps and administrators to attend the dedication of the golden statue he has erected — which shows their political importance and proximity to royal power.

2. More broadly, it is an advisor or royal officer whose role combines judgment (settling disputes) and counsel (providing advice to the king on matters of the kingdom). The context in which these figures appear alongside treasurers and legal experts suggests a major administrative role.
H0148.origine: The word is of Persian origin, composed of two elements: "adar" (great, chief) and "gaz" or "gar" (chief, magistrate, which appears in other Persian administrative titles like "satrap"). Biblical Aramaic borrowed it to designate dignitaries of the Persian and Babylonian court, reflecting the direct contact of the Hebrews with these empires.
H0148.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Bible, both passages in Daniel 3:2 and 3:3, in the account of the dedication of the golden statue. The Segond translates it as "great" judges to emphasize the high rank of these magistrates. The word is part of an impressive list of official titles (satraps, administrators, governors, treasurers, legal experts, magistrates), highlighting the grandeur of the ceremony and the seriousness with which the king summons the elites of his administration.
H0148.portee: This term reminds us that even in a pagan kingdom, justice and the counsel of the wise are valued and structured. For Daniel and his companions, these Babylonian magistrates represent the political order against which faith in God alone remains the ultimate test — as illustrated by the refusal of the three young men to bow down before the statue, despite the presence of all this authority.

sens: With accuracy, without error
With speed and without delay
With care and diligence
In a conscientious and faithful manner
H0149.detail:
1. The word primarily expresses the idea of accuracy: doing something correctly, without mistake, precisely according to what is requested. It is to accomplish a task as it should be done, point by point.
2. It also carries the idea of promptness and regularity: acting without delay, doing things at the right time. The king must ensure that the offering is sent on time, without delay.
3. The adverb suggests conscientious application, as if one puts heart and attention into it. In Ezra 7:23, the scribe Ezra asks that the orders of the God of heaven concerning the temple be carried out with the jealous care that appeases divine anger.
4. Finally, it designates faithfulness in execution: honoring commitments, fulfilling duties without negligence, for the good of those one serves.
H0149.origine: This rare Aramaic word in the Bible likely comes from a root expressing the idea of care and vigilance. It appears in the Persian context where administrative precision and promptness were emphasized values. The word belongs to the Aramaic portion of the book of Ezra, which reflects the atmosphere of the Persian empire's chancelleries, where the formulation of orders required accuracy and clarity.
H0149.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 7:23. The Persian king Artaxerxes orders Ezra to restore the worship of the temple in Jerusalem according to the Law of God. He asks that everything be done "punctually" — that is, exactly according to the prescriptions, quickly, and with the peace of mind that the order will be executed faithfully. It is an administrative term, characteristic of the style of official decrees reported in the book of Ezra.
H0149.portee: For the reader, this word reminds us that God is a God of order and precision. When the Bible asks that the things of God be done "punctually," it teaches that worship, prayer, and obedience deserve our scrupulous attention and promptness. It is an invitation to serve God with accuracy and faithfulness, without negligence or carelessness.

sens: Persian gold coin of high weight
H0150.detail: 1. The darique is a gold coin of great value, used in the Persian empire. Its weight was standardized (approximately 4.32 grams). In 1 Chronicles 29:7, the contributions to the Temple include "ten thousand dariques" of gold, showing that it was a prestigious currency for the most significant donations. In Ezra 8:27, "twenty gold bowls worth a thousand dariques" indicates that dariques were also used to assess the value of precious items.
H0150.origine: The Hebrew word אֲדַרְכֹּן comes from the Old Persian *dari-ka, literally meaning "royal" or "of the king," as this coin was minted by the Persian king Darius I. It bears the name of the monarch who created it. It is a borrowing from Persian into the Jewish world of the post-exilic period, when the Judeans lived under Persian rule.
H0150.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, solely in the books of Ezra and Chronicles (post-exilic period, 5th century B.C.). Both instances concern donations to the Temple: dariques as contributions to the service of the House of God (1 Chronicles 29:7), and as a measure of the value of gold offerings (Ezra 8:27). The context suggests that it was a reference monetary unit in the Persian administration and in the transactions of the Judeans after the Exile.
H0150.portee: The darique reminds the reader that the people of God lived under foreign powers, and that their gifts to the Temple were expressed in the currencies of the time. It is a sign of the faithfulness of the Judeans returning from exile: they generously give with Persian gold to rebuild the House of God. This historical detail also demonstrates the authenticity of the biblical accounts, which do not hide Judah's political dependence.

sens: Officer of King David, in charge of taxes
Officer of King Rehoboam, responsible for tax collection, stoned during the Northern revolt
H0151.detail:
1. Adoram is a historical figure from the Old Testament who served King David as an administrator responsible for collecting taxes from the kingdom (2 Samuel 20:24). This was an important role in the royal administration, requiring the management of the country's resources for the king and the government.
2. After David's death, Adoram continued to serve as an officer under King Rehoboam, son and successor of Solomon. When Rehoboam imposed burdens too heavy on the people of the North, it provoked a revolt: the king sent Adoram to try to restore order, but the angry crowd stoned him to death (1 Kings 12:18). This event marks the beginning of the division between the Northern kingdom (Israel) and the Southern kingdom (Judah).
H0151.origine: The name Adoram means in Hebrew "my Lord is exalted." It is a compound of the word "Adon" (Lord) and the root "ram" (to be exalted, lifted up). This name reflects the piety of his parents and their respect for God. In the Bible, Adoram is also called Adoniram or Hadoram according to parallel texts.
H0151.emploi: Adoram appears twice in the Bible, at two key moments in the history of the Israelite monarchy. First under David (2 Samuel 20:24), as a reliable officer in the royal administration. Then under Rehoboam (1 Kings 12:18), where he inadvertently embodies the cause of the kingdom's division: sent to collect taxes from the revolting Northern tribes, he becomes the victim of their anger and dies stoned. His role illustrates how royal decisions regarding taxes could trigger serious political crises.
H0151.portee: The story of Adoram reminds Christian readers that even loyal servants are not immune to the consequences of poor political decisions. It also shows how pride and injustice (Rehoboam's excessive taxes) can incite revolt and cause lasting divisions. It is an example of the fragility of human kingdoms in the face of refusal to govern with wisdom and fairness.

sens: Foreign deity worshiped by the Sepharvites
Son of the Assyrian king Sennacherib who killed him
H0152G.detail:
1. Adrammélec is a god of the Sepharvites, a people from Mesopotamia whom the Assyrian king Shalmaneser V had settled in Israel (2 Kings 17:31). These inhabitants burned their children as sacrifices to honor Adrammélec and another deity called Anammelech, showing how important and powerful this cult was considered by its worshipers.
2. Adrammélec is also the name of a son of Sennacherib, king of Assyria, who assassinated his father. It is one of the few cases in the Bible where the same name designates both an idol and a historical person.
H0152G.origine: The name means "honor of the king" or "Adar is prince," where Adar was a Mesopotamian deity. It is a compound formed from a divine name (Adar) and a word meaning "king" or "prince." The word reflects the religious culture of the ancient Near Eastern peoples, where the names of gods and humans often shared the same roots and honored the same celestial powers.
H0152G.emploi: Adrammélec appears only once in the Segond (2 Kings 17:31) in the context of the religious reforms of King Hezekiah and the Assyrian threat. The passage lists the foreign deities that the deported peoples in Israel worshiped, showing how the worship of the true God was threatened by the infiltration of foreign beliefs. The name reminds us that behind every idolatry lies a spiritual power that the Scriptures warn against worshiping.
H0152G.portee: The mention of Adrammélec warns the believer against compromising with the beliefs of the world. The fact that parents burned their children in his honor shows how far idolatry drives humanity away from truth and morality. It is a reminder that turning away from the living God opens the door to practices contrary to His nature and will.

sens: Son of the Assyrian king Sennacherib
Murderer of his father with his brother Sharezer
Prince or deity of the Assyrian pantheon
H0152H.detail:
1. Adrammélec is the name of an Assyrian prince, son of the powerful king Sennacherib. He appears alongside his brother Sharezer in the parallel accounts of 2 Kings and Isaiah, at the time when the king of Assyria is praying in the temple of his god Nisroch.
2. With his brother, Adrammélec murders his father Sennacherib by striking him with the sword, then flees to the land of Ararat to escape retribution. This act of regicide marks a dramatic turning point in Assyrian political history.
3. The name Adrammélec literally means "honor of the king" or "Adar is prince" (Adar being an Assyrian deity). This meaning reflects the religious and political importance that the Assyrians attached to this figure and the context of their divine pantheon.
H0152H.origine: The name Adrammélec is of Assyrian origin. It combines two elements: "Adar," the name of a major deity of the Assyro-Babylonian pantheon associated with war and judgment, and an element meaning "prince" or "honor." This name reflects the common practice in ancient Mesopotamia of giving royal children names that referenced the gods and royal virtues. The name appears only in the two parallel passages of the Old Testament that report the fall of Sennacherib.
H0152H.emploi: Adrammélec appears only twice in the Bible, in the parallel passages of 2 Kings 19:37 and Isaiah 37:38, both recounting the same historical event: the murder of King Sennacherib. These two accounts are identical in their essential terms, confirming the historical significance of the reported fact. Adrammélec is presented as a son of the great king of Assyria who, after striking his father in the temple of Nisroch, flees to Ararat with his brother Sharezer, while their younger brother Esarhaddon takes power. The account highlights the political instability even within the Assyrian power that threatens Judah.
H0152H.portee: The account of the murder of Sennacherib by his own sons shows that even the greatest kings and the strongest earthly powers remain subject to divine Providence. This event occurs directly after God delivers Judah by destroying the Assyrian army (2 Kings 19:35), revealing how the Lord can bring down human pride through unexpected means. The fall of Sennacherib and the rise of Esarhaddon remind the believer that the plans of men, even the most powerful, are subject to divine will.

sens: Act of brute force, coercion exercised against someone to subdue them
Power, physical force or authority used oppressively
H0153.detail:
1. Violence here refers to the brutal use of force to impose one's will. In Ezra 4:23, the adversaries of the Jews "stopped their work by violence and force": they used physical coercion or threats to halt the reconstruction of the Temple.
2. The word refers to power or authority exercised in an oppressive or tyrannical manner — the ability to coerce by force, without regard for law or justice.
H0153.origine: The Aramaic word אֶדְרַע (edraʿ) comes from a root common to ancient Semitic languages. It is directly related to the Hebrew זְרוֹעַ (zeroaʿ, "arm" or "force"), since the arm is the instrument of strength and power. This image of the striking or controlling arm is the origin of the figurative sense of oppressive power.
H0153.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezra 4:23, in the Aramaic context of royal correspondence with the Persian king Artaxerxes. It denotes the action by which the authorities of the kingdom forced the Jews to abandon the reconstruction of the Temple in Jerusalem. The political and administrative context emphasizes that this violence is not an isolated act, but the use of official authority to coerce and oppress.
H0153.portee: This word reminds us that any domination based on brute force is a form of evil, especially when it opposes God's purposes. For the reader, it invites recognition of how institutional or political violence can paralyze God's work, and to place trust not in the power of men, but in divine sovereignty.

sens: Capital of the kingdom of Bashan in northern Transjordan
Fortified city where Og, king of Bashan, established his royal residence
Site of a decisive battle between Israel and Og, king of the Rephaim
H0154.detail:
1. Edrei is a principal city of Bashan, a kingdom located north of the Jabbok, in Transjordan. Its name means "good pasture" in Hebrew, reflecting the fertility of this region. It is a city on the eastern plateau, in the territory that the Israelites conquered upon entering Canaan.

2. Edrei served as the royal residence for Og, king of Bashan. Moses fought against Og and his people there to conquer this territory (Numbers 21:33; Deuteronomy 3:1). The city is among the strongholds of the kingdom of Bashan, alongside Ashtaroth.

3. After its conquest by Israel, Edrei enters into the territorial inheritance of Israel. It is listed with other cities of the kingdom of Og: it marks the eastern boundary of the conquered territory with Salcah (Deuteronomy 3:10).

4. Edrei and Ashtaroth are mentioned together as the two capitals of the kingdom of Bashan, residences of the last king of the Rephaim before Moses defeated him (Joshua 12:4; Joshua 13:12).
H0154.origine: The name "Edrei" comes from the Hebrew אֶדְרְעִי (edreî) and literally means "good pasture." It reflects the pastoral and fertile nature of the region of Bashan, known for its abundant grazing lands and prosperous flocks. This type of Hebrew geographical name often describes the character or wealth of the place.
H0154.emploi: Edrei appears 8 times in the Bible, primarily in the account of the conquest of Transjordan by Moses and Israel. It is mentioned as the site of the pivotal battle where Moses defeated Og, king of Bashan (Numbers 21:33; Deuteronomy 3:1). It is then regularly included in the listings of cities and territorial boundaries of the conquered kingdom of Bashan (Deuteronomy 3:10; Joshua 12:4; Joshua 13:12). It is always a major city of the kingdom of Og, shared with Ashtaroth as an administrative or military center. Its repeated mention underscores its strategic and political importance in the region.

sens: Outer garment, generally loose, worn over other clothes
Piece of fabric or fur of fine quality, sign of dignity or function
Splendor, magnificence, particular brilliance of a person or thing
H0155.detail:
1. The mantle is a garment that envelops the body, worn over other clothing. In Genesis 25:25, the newborn Esau comes out of the womb "covered like a mantle" with red hair — the image suggests something that envelops, that covers. It is an everyday garment, but imposing and visible.

2. The mantle becomes an object of power and authority. When Elijah throws his mantle on Elisha (1 Kings 19:19), this gesture inaugurates the prophet: the mantle is the mark of the prophet, his badge, his spiritual uniform. Elisha picks it up after Elijah's death (2 Kings 2:13) as one would take up a succession. It is a garment that confers identity, a mission.

3. The mantle symbolizes splendor and magnificence. When Ezekiel speaks of a "magnificent" vine (Ezekiel 17:8) or Zechariah of the "magnificence" of the shepherds (Zechariah 11:3), the word does not describe a garment, but glory, brilliance, that which makes something imposing and beautiful. It is the impression of greatness and nobility that something inspires.
H0155.origine: The Hebrew word adéret comes from a root that evokes thickness, fullness, magnificence. It primarily denotes something ample and rich — a fabric that envelops. The concrete sense of the mantle (luxurious garment) then extends to the figurative sense of splendor, brilliance: that which adorns a person or thing with beauty and prestige, just as a mantle covers the body. Translations also refer to "glory" to denote this particular brilliance.
H0155.emploi: The word appears about a dozen times in the Old Testament, primarily in narrative prose. It first denotes a material garment: the wool or fur mantle thrown over the shoulders (1 Kings 19:19; 2 Kings 2:13), like that of Achan taken as plunder (Joshua 7:24). The prophet's mantle becomes a badge: when Elijah throws it on Elisha, this gesture constitutes the successor. Gradually, the word shifts to the figurative: the "magnificent" vine of Ezekiel 17:8, the "magnificence" of the shepherds in Zechariah 11:3. Through these uses, the word moves from the material to the spiritual, from the visible garment to the invisible prestige.
H0155.portee: For the believer, Elijah's mantle reminds us that the prophetic calling is not a personal burden, but a transmission, a spiritual inheritance received and entrusted to others. It also symbolizes how God clothes those He calls with a new identity. The magnificence invites recognition that true splendor — that which comes from God — fades and disappears if separated from its source: the magnificent vine perished, the magnificence of the shepherds was destroyed. It is a lesson on the ephemeral nature of earthly glory.

sens: To feel a personal affection for someone: parent, friend, spouse, or companion
To have a marked taste for something: an object, an activity, a condition
To love God, obey Him, and worship Him with all one's heart
The love that God has for His people and His creatures, His benevolent attention
To be attached to someone to the point of not wanting to leave them
To cherish what is right, good, or wise
H0157G.detail:
1. To feel affection for a person: it is a bond of the heart that forms between beings. Isaac was the son that Abraham "loved" (Genesis 22:2), just as Jacob "loved" Rachel more than Leah (Genesis 29:30), and David "loved" Jonathan with all his heart (1 Samuel 18:1). This is familial love, friendship, marital tenderness.
2. To have a taste or appetite for something: to desire to possess or practice it. One who "loves" quarrels is one who seeks them out, who delights in them (Proverbs 17:19). A slave who "loved" his master refused freedom (Deuteronomy 15:16).
3. To love God means to devote one's whole heart to Him, to keep His commandments, and to live in dependence on Him. Moses commands Israel: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart" (Deuteronomy 6:5), and this bond of love is the cement of the covenant.
4. God Himself "loves" Israel (Deuteronomy 10:15) and His elect with a tenderness that is unique to Him: this divine favor is free and constant, choosing the people and protecting them (Deuteronomy 7:13).
5. To be attached to someone to the point of refusing separation: the slave who "loved" his master asked to remain with him (Exodus 21:5).
6. To cherish what is good and just: "To love justice" or "to love blessing" means to make it one's desire and hope, in contrast to cursing and doing evil (Psalms 33:5, Psalms 109:17).
H0157G.origine: The verb "to love" (ahav) is one of the most vibrant roots of biblical Hebrew. It primarily expresses a feeling of the heart that leads to choosing, desiring, and drawing closer. The word "friend" (ohev) is its natural derivative, designating one who loves or one who is loved. This root resonates throughout the Bible: from the cry of the heart of the servant who "loves" to the depths of the Father's love for His people, it paints the personal bond that unites beings or unites them to God.
H0157G.emploi: The verb "to love" appears more than 180 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is first encountered in the familial narratives of Genesis, where it describes intimate affections: Isaac loved by Abraham, Rachel preferred by Jacob, Benjamin cherished by his father. In the laws (Leviticus, Deuteronomy), it characterizes the central commandment: "You shall love your neighbor as yourself" (Leviticus 19:18), and more fundamentally, the love of God, which is the heart of the covenant. In the Psalms and Wisdom literature, the word expands: one "loves" justice, mercy, life itself. God's love for His people or for Israel is consistently referenced in liturgy and prophetic prediction (Jeremiah, Hosea), to remind of the unshakeable covenant. The word can also describe sinful attachments: Samson "loved" Delilah, Solomon "loved" many foreign women (1 Kings 11:1). The context, the object, and the subject of love thus reveal the orientation of the heart.
H0157G.portee: This word opens to the reader the mystery of the human heart and that of God. It shows that faith is not a cold obedience, but a relationship of love: to love the Lord with all one's heart is the first commandment and the summary of the Law. Conversely, seeing what we "love" or what we seek reveals our true nature and our true gods. Finally, discovering that God "loves" His people, despite their unfaithfulness, is to grasp one of the greatest comforts of faith: I am loved by the One who can do all, and this love is primary, eternal, and unconditional.

sens: To feel affection for a person (parent, spouse, friend)
To desire something intensely (food, rest, wisdom)
To cherish God or His justice
To have the favor or friendship of someone
The love of God for mankind or His people
H0157H.detail:
1. To love is to feel a deep affection for someone: a parent, a spouse, a friend. It is to seek their good, to desire their presence. The enemies who love the Lord are compared to the sun in its strength (Judges 5:31), an image of those who shine through their faithfulness.
2. To love is also to intensely desire something: food, drink, rest, wisdom. It is an inclination of the heart toward what attracts us.
3. To love God or to love justice is to cherish what comes from Him, to give these realities a central place in one's life.
4. To be a friend of someone is to maintain a relationship of trust and loyalty with them. The friends of the rich are many (Proverbs 14:20), but only a true friend dares to hurt you for your correction (Proverbs 27:6).
5. The Lord loves His people, particularly Israel: it is His free, unwavering love that precedes any human response. Abraham is called the friend of God (Isaiah 41:8) because the Lord chose him and loved him with an elect friendship.
H0157H.origine: This Hebrew verb expresses affection and attachment in the broadest sense. Its root evokes the inclination of the heart toward someone or something. The word also produces names: friend (one who is loved or one who loves), love. The verb appears in all senses of personal relationship, intimate desire, and divine election.
H0157H.emploi: The verb to love is very frequent in the Hebrew Bible. It first denotes ordinary human affection: marital love, familial love, or friendship (Esther 5:10, where Haman summons his friends). It also expresses the appetites of the heart: one loves food, rest, wisdom. But it takes on a spiritual significance when it speaks of love for God or His justice (Psalms 38:12). Finally, it reveals the electing love of the Lord: God loves Israel (2 Chronicles 20:7), He loves Abraham as a friend (Isaiah 41:8), He loves justice. In all cases, it is an attachment of the heart that engages the whole person.
H0157H.portee: This word teaches us that love, in the Bible, is never a mere fleeting emotion: it is an orientation of the heart that translates into actions and faithfulness. God loves us not because we deserve it, but by pure grace, as He loved Abraham. We are called to love God and to love one another with this true love, the kind that is even manifested in fraternal correction.

sens: Feeling of deep affection and attachment
Beloved person
Relationship of friendship or alliance
H0158.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes love in the sense of the sentiment that binds two beings — an affection, an attachment. Proverbs 5:19 speaks of a woman's "loves," the attraction and tenderness she inspires in her husband, inviting him to remain captivated by her charms.
2. The word can also refer to the beloved person themselves, the one towards whom this attachment is felt. Thus, it can be used in the plural to speak of multiple beloveds or different forms of love.
3. By extension, the word takes on the meaning of friend or ally — someone with whom one is bound by a relationship of trust and goodwill. Hosea 8:9 denounces the Ephraimites who seek "friends" (allies) in Assyria, showing that love can denote a political or diplomatic relationship, a bond of alliance rather than the affection of the heart.
H0158.origine: The Hebrew word ahav (אהב) comes from a root that expresses the action of loving — the verb "to love" from which this noun is derived. This root is very ancient in Hebrew and is connected to the fundamental idea of attachment and bond between two beings. It is found throughout the Bible to speak of human love, familial love, marital love, and God's love for His people.
H0158.emploi: The word appears twice in the provided usages. In Proverbs 5:19, it evokes marital love — the "loves" of a wife, that is, her tenderness and attraction for her husband. In Hosea 8:9, it takes on a political hue: Ephraim seeks "friends" (allies) in Assyria, which shows how the same word can shift from personal sentiment to diplomatic relationship. The context of Proverbs values marital love as a treasure, while that of Hosea denounces its abuse when it is diverted towards human alliances rather than towards God.
H0158.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the different forms of love: marital love in its intensity (Proverbs), but also to discern where we place our true alliances and affections. For the Christian, it reminds us that love is a vital force, a bond that unites, but that it must be directed wisely — towards God first, then towards others in justice.

sens: Sensual and carnal pleasure
Object of physical love
Carnal passionate love
H0159.detail:
1. Pleasure denotes sensual enjoyment, particularly the physical and carnal attraction between a man and a woman. It is a feeling of intense desire and sensory enjoyment. In Proverbs 7:18, a seductive woman invites her lover to "be intoxicated with love" and to "joyfully indulge in pleasure," an image of passionate and unrestrained intimacy.
2. The word can also refer to the very object of this carnal desire — the beloved person of a purely physical love. This is why the Segond translates literally as "pleasure" rather than "love," to clearly indicate that it is not about deep affection but about sensual desire.
3. In this context of Proverbs, pleasure represents unrestrained passionate love, devoid of wisdom and respect for sacred bonds (marriage, fidelity). It is the pleasure that misleads and seduces.
H0159.origine: The Hebrew word אֹהַב comes from the root אהב (ahab), which means "to love." But here, the nominal form designates the object or fruit of that love, particularly carnal love. The same root produces other forms for "love," "lover," "friend." The richness of the Hebrew vocabulary for love allows for a distinction between familial affection, deep friendship, and physical desire — the latter being what this form of the word captures.
H0159.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Proverbs 7:18. It is found in a warning passage: an adulterous woman attempts to seduce a naive young man by inviting him to indulge in pleasure with her. The book of Proverbs, which is a collection of practical wisdom, uses this word to show the danger of carnal desire, which blinds discernment and diverts from the path of wisdom.
H0159.portee: This word invites the reader to honestly examine the forces of seduction and carnal desire, not out of prudery but with clarity. The Bible does not condemn pleasure within marriage, but it warns: pleasure alone, without true love or faithful commitment, diverts and destroys. It reminds us that sensory pleasure, while good in itself within the limits set by God, becomes a trap when it becomes master instead of servant.

sens: Deep affection between two people
Attachment of a man to a woman, romantic feeling
Sexual desire, carnal ardor
Friendship or camaraderie among close ones
Attachment of the people to their idols
God's love for His people
H0160.detail:
1. Love is the affection that unites two beings: it is what Jacob feels for Rachel, which makes him serve seven years as if they were only a few days (Genesis 29:20).

2. Between a man and a woman, it denotes the romantic feeling that can ignite: the Song of Songs celebrates it as an invincible force, "strong as death," a "flame of the Lord" (Song of Songs 8:6).

3. It also expresses physical desire and carnal attraction, as that which Amnon first feels for Tamar before it transforms into violent aversion (2 Samuel 13:15).

4. It is also the fraternal bond or faithful friendship: David and Jonathan are united by a deep "love" that surpasses the love of women (2 Samuel 1:26).

5. The Bible speaks of the "love" that the Israelites have for idols, showing that this feeling can be turned towards evil (Jeremiah 2:33).

6. God feels "love" for His people: He loved them not for their merits, but with an everlasting love that brought them out of Egypt (Deuteronomy 7:8; Jeremiah 31:3).
H0160.origine: The word הָבַה (have) literally means "to incline towards, to lean towards," the idea of turning entirely towards someone or something. The prefix אַ gives אַהֲבָה: it is the action of turning with one's whole being towards another. The root is linked to the image of a complete orientation of the heart. This word appears mainly in the poetry and wisdom literature of the Old Testament, and it is the term that Greek translators use to translate the Hebrew word when speaking of human and divine love.
H0160.emploi: The word appears 35 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical narratives (Samuel, Kings) and in poetic literature (Song of Songs, Proverbs, Prophets). It describes human love in all its dimensions: marital love (Jacob and Rachel, the Song of Songs), warrior love between warriors (David and Jonathan), parental love, and also guilty attachments (love of idols, love of evil). The word also expresses divine love towards Israel, particularly in the prophets Jeremiah and Hosea, who present God loving His people despite their unfaithfulness. Each context nuances the word: sometimes it is tranquil affection, sometimes burning passion, sometimes unwavering commitment.
H0160.portee: This word helps the Christian see that love is a fundamental force of life, neither shameful nor to be stifled, but to be ordered. The Song of Songs shows that love between spouses reflects something divine; the love that God has for His people, despite their unfaithfulness, reveals His inexhaustible grace and invites the reader to respond with a trusting and faithful love.

sens: Son of Simeon and grandson of Jacob
H0161.detail: Ohad is a man from the tribe of Simeon, one of the twelve children of Israel. He is the son of Simeon and the grandson of Jacob. His name literally means "united" or "he who unites," but the Bible does not provide any particular explanation for this name. He appears only in the genealogies that list the descendants of Simeon during the descent into Egypt.
H0161.origine: The name Ohad (אֹהַד) means "united" in Hebrew. It belongs to the family of the twelve sons of Simeon, several of whom have distinct names: Jemuel, Jamin, Jachin, Zerah, and Shaul. Like the other children of Simeon, Ohad represents one of the branches of this ancient tribe.
H0161.emploi: Ohad is mentioned only twice in the Bible, both times in genealogical lists: in Genesis 46:10 and Exodus 6:15. These two passages list the sons of Simeon who entered Egypt with Jacob. These lists are nearly identical and serve to establish the origins of the families of Simeon during ancient Egypt. Ohad is never mentioned in other contexts, nor does he play any particular role in biblical narratives.

sens: Cry of astonishment, surprise, or concern
Cry of pain or distress
Cry of indignation or protest in the face of misfortune
Heartfelt call to God in urgency
H0162.detail:
1. It is an interjection that expresses astonishment at something unexpected or troubling to the speaker. Jeremiah says, "Ah! Lord God!" upon learning that he must prophesy, seized by the surprise of this call (Jeremiah 1:6).
2. It can also manifest immediate suffering: Jephthah's son cries, "Ah! my daughter!" upon seeing his only daughter come to meet him, knowing he cannot revoke his vow (Judges 11:35).
3. The word expresses indignation at misfortune or loss: the prophet exclaims, "Ah!" when he discovers that the iron of an axe, borrowed, has fallen into the water and cannot be recovered (2 Kings 6:5).
4. It is also a cry from the heart that spontaneously arises when the believer turns to God in urgency or confusion: Joshua cries, "Ah! Lord God!" to ask God why He allowed Israel's defeat at Ai (Joshua 7:7).
H0162.origine: It is an interjection, meaning an exclamation that does not have a proper verbal root. It expresses a raw feeling, an immediate reaction of the body and soul — like the natural cry of the heart when it is moved. The Hebrew form אֲהָהּ (ahah) is close to other interjections of pain or surprise in Semitic languages; it functions as a kind of breath of feeling.
H0162.emploi: This word appears fifteen times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly among the prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel) and in historical narratives (Joshua, Judges, Kings). Joshua uses it to implore God in the face of defeat; Jeremiah employs it several times to express his hesitation or rebellion before the word of the Lord; the prophets use it to cry out their anguish or confusion. In each case, "ah" is the cry of the heart that precedes a supplication or objection addressed to God — it is the open door to dialogue with Him.
H0162.portee: This interjection teaches us that God welcomes our cries and raw questions, our feelings of astonishment or distress. It shows that prayer does not need perfect formulas: the psalmist or the prophet can simply cry out "Ah!" and turn to God, who hears the cry of the heart. It is an invitation to authenticity in our dialogue with Him.

sens: River of Babylon
Gathering place for exiles
H0163.detail: Ahava is a river located in Babylon, in the region where the exiled Jews lived after the destruction of the temple in Jerusalem. It is near this river that the priest Ezra gathered the Jews who wished to return to Jerusalem (Ezra 8:15).
H0163.origine: The name literally means "I will survive" in Hebrew. Ahava likely refers to a river or canal in the Babylonian river system, perhaps a tributary or a canal of the Euphrates. The name may reflect the importance of this place as a vital water point for survival and passage.
H0163.emploi: Ahava appears only three times in the Bible, all in the book of Ezra in chapter 8. It serves as a strategic gathering point: it is there that Ezra gathers the exiles who want to return to Jerusalem, where he proclaims a fast to ask God for protection on the journey (Ezra 8:21), and from where the caravan sets out for Jerusalem (Ezra 8:31). The river Ahava thus marks the beginning of the return from exile.
H0163.portee: Ahava symbolizes the transition point between exile and return to Jerusalem, between distance from the temple and spiritual renewal. This place reminds us how God accompanies His people in their movements: it is there that Ezra turns to God through fasting, and it is from there that the hand of God protects the journey. For the Christian reader, Ahava evokes the turning points in faith where one entrusts oneself into God's hands.

sens: A judge of Israel from the tribe of Benjamin
A deliverer who freed Israel from Moabite oppression
A left-handed man and military strategist
H0164G.detail:
1. Ehud is an Israelite judge from the tribe of Benjamin, called by God to save His people. According to Judges 3:15, the Lord raised him up as a deliverer when the children of Israel cried out to Him, oppressed by the Moabite king Eglon.
2. His liberating action is remarkable: he entered alone into Eglon's palace with a concealed sword, pretending to bring a message from God (Judges 3:20), then he killed the king (Judges 3:21). He then escaped and rallied Israel to revolt (Judges 3:26-27), which allowed Israel to defeat the Moabites.
3. Ehud was distinguished by his left-handedness: he was left-handed in a context where this was exceptional, which allowed him to conceal his sword on the right side without raising suspicion (Judges 3:16 and 3:21). This physical characteristic became a tactical advantage in fulfilling his mission of liberation.
H0164G.origine: The name Ehud means "I will give thanks" or "I will be praised," expressing an act of gratitude toward God. Another interpretation connects it to the idea of "union" or "indivisibility." It is a typically Hebrew name that reflects the spirituality of the character: one who praises the Lord becomes His instrument of deliverance for the people.
H0164G.emploi: Ehud appears only in the account of Judges 3:15-26, one of the most famous stories of the judges of Israel. He is presented as the second judge after Othniel, intervening after Othniel's death when Israel fell back under the yoke of Eglon, king of Moab. His story occupies a central place in the cycle of judges as it illustrates how God uses ordinary, even physically atypical, characters to accomplish His purposes. The narrative highlights his strategic boldness, obedience to God, and effectiveness: after his action, the land had peace for eighty years (Judges 3:30).
H0164G.portee: The story of Ehud teaches the believer that God does not need superhuman strength or ordinary resources to deliver His people. What the world considers a weakness or limitation — here, the inability to use the right hand — God can transform into an instrument of victory. Ehud also shows that authentic trust in God and concrete obedience produce lasting fruit: the peace that followed his victory lasted eighty years, a remarkably long period in the tumultuous history of the judges.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the time of the divided monarchy
Son of Bilhan
H0164H.detail:
1. Ehud is a man of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned in the genealogy of the descendants of Jediael. He is listed among the sons of Bilhan, alongside his brothers Jeusch, Benjamin, Kenaana, Zethan, Tarsis, and Achishachar (1 Chronicles 7:10).
2. As a son of Bilhan, he belongs to the important genealogical line of Benjamin, one of the twelve tribes of Israel.
H0164H.origine: The name Ehud means "I will give thanks" or "I will be praised," expressing an act of recognition towards God. It can also mean "union" or "not divided." It is a Hebrew name borne by several individuals in the Old Testament, reflecting the importance of praise and unity in the Israelite tradition.
H0164H.emploi: Ehud is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:10, in a genealogical list of the tribe of Benjamin. He is presented as one of the sons of Bilhan during the counting of the descendants and family leaders of this tribe. This passage is part of the genealogical records in the book of Chronicles, which trace the origins of Israelite families during the time of the divided monarchy.

sens: question about the place
H0165.detail: 1. This word expresses a question about the place, the location where something or someone is found. It is the fundamental interrogative adverb for locating in space. In Hosea 13:10, the prophet exclaims, "Where then is your king?" to challenge Israel about the absence of their savior at the time of judgment.
H0165.origine: This Hebrew interrogative adverb is formed from the root that expresses the notion of "where" or "which place." It belongs to the family of fundamental interrogative words in Hebrew (like "who?" and "what?"), essential for asking a question about place or direction.
H0165.emploi: This word appears twice in the book of Hosea (13:10 and 13:14), in a context of reproach and divine judgment. The prophet uses it to challenge Israel by highlighting the absence of the king and savior at the critical moment of judgment. It is a rhetorical question, not a simple factual inquiry: it carries a reproach, a denunciation of Israel's unfaithfulness in rejecting God.
H0165.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the presence or absence of God in judgment: it reminds us that it is a serious question to know where our help is in spiritual crises. For Israel as well as for the Christian, the question "where?" posed by the prophet probes our trust in God.

sens: To have a luminous shine, to shine
To be remarkably clear or pure
H0166.detail: 1. To shine means to have a luminous shine, to radiate like a light. In Job 25:5, it is the moon that shines – it reflects the light of the sun in the night. 2. The word also takes on a figurative meaning: to shine is to be remarkably clear, pure, without blemish. Job 25:5 uses it to say that even the moon is not pure and clear enough in God's eyes – it pales before His absolute holiness.
H0166.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of clarity and luminosity. It evokes the image of a source or surface that reflects light, distinguished by its brightness. It is a simple yet poetic verb, frequent in the description of celestial phenomena and spiritual qualities.
H0166.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in the poetic context of the book of Job. Bildad argues that even the most luminous celestial bodies – the moon and stars – are not pure enough to rival divine holiness. Its use is therefore theological: it serves to express the incomparable purity and glory of God in contrast to creation.
H0166.portee: This word invites us to meditate on divine transcendence. God's purity is so absolute that it overshadows even what shines the most in this world – the moon and stars. This humbles the believer and encourages them to seek their own purity not in themselves, but in Christ, who alone can make us acceptable before the Father.

sens: To set up or establish a tent in a lasting way
To settle somewhere, establish one's camp or temporary dwelling
To settle, to live in a place, even temporarily
H0167.detail:
1. The concrete meaning of the verb is to set up a tent: it is the physical action of raising the fabric and stakes to create a shelter. Lot "pitched his tents toward Sodom" (Genesis 13:12) as he settled in the plain with his goods and family.
2. The verb also evokes the idea of settling in one place and living there: when Abram "lifted his tents and came to dwell by the oaks of Mamre" (Genesis 13:18), he changes his campsite, which implies a form of residence, even nomadic.
3. In a figurative sense, to pitch one's tent becomes a way of saying "to dwell" or "to reside," including for peoples: in Isaiah 13:20, it is predicted that "the Arab will not pitch his tent there," meaning that no one will inhabit or settle there anymore.
H0167.origine: The Hebrew verb אָהַל (ahal) comes from a root that evokes the idea of covering or sheltering, hence the action of pitching a tent. The tent (אֹהֶל, ohel) is the natural dwelling of Middle Eastern nomads; this verb reflects the lifestyle of the patriarchs and Bedouins, for whom the tent was the usual dwelling, often temporary but real. The same verb can also mean "to remove" or "to take down" a tent, depending on the context.
H0167.emploi: The verb אָהַל appears three times in the provided biblical usages, all in the sense of pitching or placing a tent. In Genesis, it describes the installation of the patriarchs in Canaan: Lot settles in the plain with his tents (13:12), while Abram changes camp to dwell near Mamre (13:18). In Isaiah 13:20, on the contrary, the verb is used negatively to announce desolation: the Arab will no longer pitch his tent in that place, an image of complete abandonment of the territory. The verb thus always refers to human installation, whether current or prophetically denied.
H0167.portee: This verb reminds us that in the Bible, the tent is much more than just a shelter: it is the symbol of the nomadic life of the believer, the pilgrim who acts in faith. The patriarchs pitch their tents while awaiting the promised possession; this image speaks to the Christian reader of the provisional nature of our earthly existence and our journey toward the eternal dwelling that God prepares for us.

sens: portable dwelling made of fabric and stakes, that can be moved
home, dwelling, stable or symbolic house
the tabernacle, the mobile sanctuary of Israel where God met with His people
H0168G.detail:
1. The tent is primarily a portable dwelling, typical of nomadic life: it is set up and taken down according to movements. In Genesis 4:20, it speaks of "those who dwell in tents" as shepherds who follow their flocks. It is a house made of fabric and stakes, which can be transported from one place to another.
2. By extension, the word designates any home or dwelling, even a stable one. When Joshua sends the tribes back and they return "to their tents" (Joshua 22:6), it refers to their permanent homes or their regions of origin — the image of the tent evokes the idea of home, of belonging.
3. The "tent of meeting" (also called the "tent of the Encounter") is the tabernacle, the mobile sanctuary of Israel during the desert. It is where sacrifices were brought (Leviticus 1:3), where the Lord met His people (Exodus 29:42-44), and where His presence resided. This portable structure was made of goat hair curtains and linen, assembled on a wooden framework.
H0168G.origine: The Hebrew word אֹהֶל (ohel) comes from a root that evokes the idea of covering oneself, of taking shelter. It is from the same family as the word "ohala" (tent in Arabic). In the Bible, this term is consistent and neutral: it simply describes the natural habitat of the nomads of the Near East, before designating God's own sanctuary. The choice of this word for the tabernacle is laden with meaning: God, who initially appears to Abram under a tent (Genesis 18:1), chooses to dwell among His people in a tent, not in a palace.
H0168G.emploi: The word "tent" appears about 300 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in Genesis and Exodus. It primarily designates the habitat of the patriarchs: Abram pitches his tent (Genesis 12:8, 13:3), and it is under a tent that he receives the three heavenly visitors (Genesis 18:1-10). In the account of the desert and the sanctuary, "tent of meeting" becomes the technical term for the tabernacle: offerings are brought there (Leviticus 1:3), the priest officiates there (Exodus 29:30, 39:32-40), and it is there that the Lord "pitches His tent" among Israel. The word thus retains a double connotation: the vulnerability of one who dwells under a tent, and the mobility of the divine presence that follows His people.
H0168G.portee: This word reminds the reader that the encounter with God does not always take place in an impressive stone edifice: it is under a simple tent that the Lord chooses to dwell among Israel during the desert. This teaches that the relationship with God is alive and portable, not tied to a fixed place, and that His presence can follow us everywhere.
