For the believer, it is an image of freedom and intimacy with God: no hierarchical distance, just a meeting under the same roof, however fragile it may be.

sens: Portable dwelling made of fabric or skin stretched over a framework, that nomads transported with them
Dwelling or home in general, house
The portable sanctuary of Israel, the sacred tent where God dwelled among His people
H0168H.detail:
1. The tent was the natural home of the nomads and shepherds of the ancient Near East. It could be taken down, transported, and set up elsewhere, making it the very symbol of itinerant life and the absence of a fixed dwelling. When the Israelites in retreat "fled each to his tent" (1 Samuel 4:10), it was to this mobile home that they ran for refuge.
2. The word also designates, more broadly, the dwelling or habitation. When Joshua "sent" the people "to their tents" (Joshua 22:7), he simply sent them home, to their residence. This is how one speaks of "returning to one's tents" in the sense of going home (1 Kings 8:66).
3. The sacred tent — the tabernacle — was the earthly dwelling of God among Israel: a special tent, built according to a divine plan, where the ark of the covenant and the altar of sacrifices were located. It embodied God's presence among His people, portable like them, following them in the desert and then into Canaan.
H0168H.origine: The Hebrew word אֹהֶל comes from a root that evokes the idea of "dwelling" or "inhabiting." The same word is used throughout the Hebrew Bible to designate both the tents of the patriarchs and nomads, the military tents of the Israelite armies, and especially the sacred tent of worship — also called the "tent of meeting" (where God met His people). It is a fundamental word for understanding Israel's spirituality: before the stone temple, it was a simple, transportable tent that manifested God's presence.
H0168H.emploi: The word appears about forty times in the Old Testament, in very varied contexts. It primarily designates the tents of the inhabitants of the desert and shepherds: Moses, Abraham, Job lived under the tent. It also describes the military tents from which kings led their armies (2 Samuel 18:17, 20:22; 2 Kings 8:21). But its most important use is religious: the sacred tent is the place of worship, the house of God. The psalms refer to it (Psalms 132:3). The meaning thus nuances from the concrete (the nomadic shelter) to the spiritual (the dwelling of God), but always with the underlying idea of a presence that remains and protects.
H0168H.portee: For the biblical reader, the word "tent" evokes God's humility: the Creator of the universe chose to dwell not in a stone palace, but under a tent, transportable and fragile, among His people. It is a lesson of divine proximity and solidarity. Before Jesus who "pitched His tent among us" (John 1:14, in Greek: the same word "dwelt"), God already dwelled this way. This image invites us not to seek God in external magnificence, but in the simplicity and intimacy of His presence.

sens: Son of Zerubbabel, of the tribe of Judah, during the time of the Divided Monarchy
H0169.detail: Ohel is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 3:20. He is a son of Zerubbabel, the leader of the exile upon returning from Babylon. His name appears in the genealogy of the descendants of Judah, among his brothers Meshullam, Hananiah, Shalomith, and others. He lived during the time of the Divided Monarchy, but the Bible reports no details about his life or deeds.
H0169.origine: The name Ohel means "tent" in Hebrew, from the word אֹהֶל derived from the ancient root designating the nomadic dwelling. It is a symbolic name, like many Hebrew names, evoking the tent or encampment. Although the meaning of the name is known, nothing in the biblical text indicates why this name was given to this man.
H0169.emploi: Ohel appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 3:20, in the list of the children of Zerubbabel. He is among nine sons listed, with no additional details provided about his life, role, or descendants. His mention in this genealogy serves solely to document the royal and priestly lineage of Judah after the Babylonian exile.

sens: The name of a prophetic woman symbolizing Samaria
The unfaithful Northern Kingdom to God, compared to an adulterous wife
Samaria delivered to Assyria through its idolatrous alliances
H0170.detail:
1. Ohola is a symbolic name given by the prophet Ezekiel to designate Samaria, the capital of the Northern Kingdom of Israel. The name literally means "her own tent" or "her own tabernacle," evoking a house established by its own strength rather than according to God's plan.
2. In Ezekiel's vision (23:4), Ohola and her sister Oholiba (Jerusalem) are presented as two women belonging to the Lord who bore Him children, then betrayed Him through infidelity. Ohola represents the Northern Kingdom that "became inflamed for her lovers, the Assyrians her neighbors" (Ezekiel 23:5), meaning that she sought political and religious alliances with Assyria instead of remaining faithful to God.
3. The fate of Ohola symbolizes judgment: like a prostitute exposed and judged, Samaria was delivered into the hands of her Assyrian lovers, who destroyed her and took her into exile (see Ezekiel 23:9-10). She becomes a terrible warning for the exiles of Judah against infidelity.
H0170.origine: The name Ohola (אׇהֳלָה) literally means "her own tent." It is formed from the Hebrew root for "tent" (אֹהֶל), with a possessive. The prophet Ezekiel chose this symbolic name to designate Samaria: unlike other kingdoms that remain under the tent of God (His temple, His covenant), Samaria had established itself in "her own tent," that is, according to her own strength and her own religious choices, without depending on God.
H0170.emploi: Ohola appears four times in chapter 23 of Ezekiel, always in a prophetic vision of judgment. Ezekiel 23:4 establishes the identity: Ohola = Samaria, and her sister Oholiba = Jerusalem. The next two verses (23:5, 23:36) describe Ohola's infidelity: she prostituted herself with Assyria, she "became inflamed for her lovers." Ezekiel 23:44 uses the stark image of the prostitute to show that Samaria, just like Jerusalem, surrendered to foreign powers like a depraved woman. This symbolic portrait reminds the exiles of Judah of the reasons for the destruction of the Northern Kingdom and warns them against the same mistakes.
H0170.portee: Ohola serves as a warning symbol for the biblical reader: it shows how a people and a kingdom can turn away from the covenant with God by seeking security and prestige from the political powers of the world. Her judgment reveals that spiritual infidelity has real and tragic consequences. For the exiles of Judah listening to Ezekiel, this prophecy reminds them that only faithfulness to God guarantees protection and survival.

sens: Craftsman and assistant to Bezalel during the construction of the tabernacle
Son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan
H0171.detail: Oholiab is a highly skilled craftsman whom God specifically chose to assist Bezalel in constructing the tabernacle in the wilderness. His name means "the tent of my father," which highlights the importance of the sanctuary in the life of the people. Like Bezalel, he receives wisdom and understanding directly from God to carry out the sacred work (Exodus 31:6). He possesses various talents: he knows how to engrave, invent patterns, and embroider on fabrics dyed in purple, blue, and scarlet (Exodus 38:23). Although he is the second name mentioned after Bezalel, he plays an essential and recognized role; Moses calls him among "all the skilled men in whom the Lord had put wisdom" (Exodus 36:2). He is from the tribe of Dan, reminding us that the talents given by God are distributed throughout Israel.
H0171.origine: The name Oholiab literally means "my tent is father" or "father of the tent" in Hebrew, a poetic expression that values the tabernacle as the dwelling of the Lord at the heart of the people. Ahisamach, his father mentioned in the same passages, means "my brother has supported." Oholiab embodies the biblical idea that artistic and technical gifts come from God and are to be used in His worship.
H0171.emploi: Oholiab appears five times in the account of the construction of the tabernacle (Exodus 31, 35, 36, 38), always in direct connection with Bezalel and the work of the sanctuary. In each mention, the emphasis is placed on his gifts: God grants him wisdom and understanding (31:6, 36:1-2), he has the gift of teaching (35:34), and he excels in the delicate techniques of engraving, invention, and embroidery (38:23). The five occurrences progressively structure the project: orders from God, calling of the workers, execution of the work. Oholiab is never alone; always associated with Bezalel, he represents the team of those whom the Lord inspires to build His dwelling.
H0171.portee: Oholiab teaches that ordinary talents—those of a craftsman, a embroiderer—are just as important in God's eyes as any spiritual gift. He shows that serving God is not limited to the priesthood or prophecy, but can be expressed through the work of hands, executed with excellence and a willing heart. His example encourages recognition of each person's gifts and putting them to service in the church and community with the same dedication that Oholiab had for the tabernacle.

sens: Tropical tree that produces a fragrant resin
Perfume or oil extracted from this tree
Precious substance used to scent clothing and places
Symbol of beauty and luxury in biblical poetry
H0174.detail:
1. Aloes is an exotic tree from which a highly sought-after aromatic resin is extracted. Balaam speaks of it as a wonder that the Lord has planted alongside majestic cedars (Numbers 24:6), highlighting its status as a noble and prestigious plant.
2. The fragrance of aloes, extracted from this tree, was used to scent clothing and precious fabrics. The psalmist describes how aloes, mixed with myrrh and cassia, perfumes royal garments (Psalms 45:9), evoking the splendor of a sovereign.
3. As a highly valued aromatic substance, aloes ranked among the finest perfumes. In the Song of Solomon, it is listed alongside spikenard, saffron, and cinnamon, testifying to its place among the most esteemed aromatics (Song of Solomon 4:14).
4. In the Bible, aloes symbolizes seduction, luxury, and earthly beauty. Those seeking to seduce resort to it as a means of sensual pleasure (Proverbs 7:17), showing how this substance was associated with worldly desires.
H0174.origine: The Hebrew word אָהָל comes from a root likely denoting wood or tree. Aloes is an imported product from Africa and South Asia, from which the Hebrews obtained it through trade with neighboring peoples. Its rarity and the cost of its importation made aloes a luxury reserved for the elite.
H0174.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always as a precious and fragrant substance. In Balaam (Numbers 24:6), it illustrates the beauty of God's blessing on Israel. In royal and romantic contexts (Psalms 45:9, Song of Solomon 4:14), it ranks among the finest perfumes adorning splendor. In Proverbs 7:17, it becomes a tool of carnal seduction, revealing how the same precious substance can serve legitimate luxury or waywardness. Its constant presence alongside other prestigious aromatics underscores the importance of perfume in ancient Near Eastern customs.
H0174.portee: Aloes reminds us that beauty and sensual pleasure, while legitimate in themselves (the psalmist celebrates royal perfumes), can divert the heart from the path of God if they become an end in themselves. Recognizing that precious things come from God invites the believer to enjoy them with gratitude and temperance, without making them idols.

sens: Brother of Moses and man of the tribe of Levi
H0175.detail: Aaron is the older brother of Moses, son of Amram and Jochebed, from the tribe of Levi (Exodus 6:20). He first appears as Moses' spokesperson before Pharaoh: "Is there not your brother Aaron, the Levite? I know that he will speak fluently" (Exodus 4:14). Along with Moses, he becomes the leader of the people during the Exodus from Egypt and the years in the desert.
H0175.origine: The name Aaron means "light bringer" or "bearer of light." His role as a spiritual light for Israel is embodied in his vocation as high priest, the one who wears the breastplate adorned with the Thummim and Urim — the "lights" of Israel that reveal God's will (Exodus 28:30).
H0175.emploi: Aaron is mentioned 343 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers. He is first the companion and spokesperson of Moses during the plagues of Egypt (Exodus 7-11). The Lord then charges him with the service of the sanctuary: he becomes the first high priest of Israel, consecrated with his sons to offer sacrifices (Leviticus 1:5). His four sons — Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar — continue the priesthood. Aaron dies on Mount Hor at the age of 123, and all Israel mourns for him for thirty days (Numbers 20:29).
H0175.portee: Aaron embodies the role of the priest: the one who stands between God and the people, who offers sacrifices, who bears the names of Israel on his heart and shoulders (Exodus 28:29). His life also shows the dangers of spiritual weakness: he makes the golden calf when Moses delays (Exodus 32), reminding us that even church leaders must remain vigilant. For Christians, Aaron prefigures Christ, the true High Priest who intercedes for us before God (Hebrews 5:4-5).

sens: Indicates the alternative between two or more possibilities
Introduces an option that excludes or replaces the previous one
Lists two elements in succession, with indifference between them
Expresses a hypothetical condition or assumption
H0176A.detail:
1. The word "or" presents a choice between several options: you can choose one or the other. In Genesis 24:49, the servant asks Rebecca's father and mother: "Declare it to me; or else, declare it to me, and I will turn to the right or to the left" — he offers two possible directions.
2. Sometimes "or" introduces a correction or a better option than the first: the second possibility takes precedence. In Leviticus 5:7 and 5:11, when a poor person cannot pay their full offering, a less costly offering is accepted "or" even simply flour — a merciful concession.
3. "Or" can also simply list two things side by side without truly opposing them. In Leviticus 13:56, the priest examines whether the sore is in "the warp or the woof" of the fabric — both parts of the fabric are mentioned together.
4. Used to express a hypothesis or an uncertain condition: "if this happens or if it does not happen." In 2 Samuel 3:35, David swears, "if I taste bread or anything before the sun goes down" — he states a feared condition.
H0176A.origine: The word "or" (אוֹ) is a short and common conjunction in Hebrew, with no special nominal root. It belongs to the class of linking words that structure thought and discourse. It is found in all contexts of choice and condition, functioning like the Greek ἤ (ê) in the New Testament.
H0176A.emploi: The word "or" appears more than 200 times in the Hebrew Bible, notably in the Torah (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy) and historical narratives (Genesis, Samuel). It is particularly frequent in the Mosaic law, where it specifies ritual and legal alternatives: which animal to offer, what fine to pay, what conditions render a person unclean. In Leviticus 13-15, the diagnosis of sores and impurity constantly employs "or" to enumerate cases: "or if... or if..." The word can also express a threat or divine condition ("you will do this or you will suffer that").
H0176A.portee: This small word manifests the practical wisdom of God's law: it does not provide a single rigid path, but often offers multiple legitimate options suited to circumstances and individual capacity. Seeing that God accepts "either this beast or that one" according to the means of the poor (Leviticus 5:7-11) teaches that God looks at the heart, not just the exact form of the sacrifice. It is an invitation to recognize that faithful faith can take various forms.

sens: Jewish man during the Exile
H0177.detail: Uel is a Jewish man mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time of the return from exile to Jerusalem. He appears in the list of men who had married foreign women during the Exile and who were to separate from them according to the decree of the governor Ezra (Ezra 10:34). His name appears among the descendants of Bani, an important family of those returning.
H0177.origine: The name Uel means "will of God" or "wish of God" in Hebrew: it combines the root that expresses divine will with the name of God (El). It is a typical theophoric name of the time, expressing the piety of the parents who gave it.
H0177.emploi: Uel appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:34, during the return of the Judeans from Babylonian captivity. He is part of the list established by Ezra of men who had transgressed the Law by taking foreign wives. This mention is set in a context of restoring the religious purity of the community returned from Exile.

sens: To practice necromancy, that is, to consult the spirits of the deceased for revelations
The person who practices this
The spirit or ghost of a dead person that one claims to bring back
A wineskin, a flask (very ancient and very rare meaning)
H0178.detail:
1. To evoke the dead means to seek to communicate with the spirits of the deceased to know the future or hidden secrets. It is a forbidden practice of divination in Israel. Saul himself, despite its prohibition, stooped to this before the battle of Mount Gilboa by consulting the woman who conjures spirits (1 Samuel 28:8).

2. The one who practices this — the woman consulted or the priest who proposes it — becomes an interlocutor of the powers of evil. The Law requires that such a person be put to death (Leviticus 20:27) because they bring moral defilement upon Israel and a rupture with the Lord.

3. The spirit or ghost that one believes to bring back is also referred to by this word. Job speaks of a wineskin swollen with empty wind, an image of those hollow voices that claim to be the dead, but are merely breath (Job 32:19).

4. Very rarely, the word designates a wineskin or flask — a swollen leather container —: an ancient meaning that has disappeared, but which testifies to the richness of the Hebrew vocabulary.
H0178.origine: The word comes from a very ancient root that suggests the idea of "hollow" or "empty" — perhaps the image of a voice coming from nothingness, a cavern, or a spectral breath. The word appears in three major biblical contexts: the Law (Leviticus, Deuteronomy), the history of the kings (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles), and the prophets (Isaiah, Job). Its usage changes little: it always denotes the forbidden act, the person who practices it, or the spiritual power involved.
H0178.emploi: The word appears sixteen times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always in a context of condemnation. Moses forbids this practice in Deuteronomy 18:11, God calls it defilement in Leviticus 19:31 and 20:27. The story of Saul in 1 Samuel 28 provides the most famous example: the king of Israel, desperate before the battle, violates his own law by asking a woman to evoke the deceased prophet Samuel. The impious kings after the Exile, such as Manasseh (2 Kings 21:6), fall back into this sin. The prophets (Isaiah) and the wise (Job) allude to it as an abomination from which Israel must purify itself.
H0178.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader of a crucial truth: the boundary between the living and the dead is closed and guarded by God alone. Consulting the dead means seeking knowledge outside of God, a spiritual rebellion. The death of Saul, directly linked to this sin (1 Chronicles 10:13), shows that rejecting the Word of God to inquire of spirits leads to divine judgment. The word invites one to place all trust in God, the unique source of truth and wisdom.

sens: man in charge of King David's camels
Ishmaelite in the service of David
H0179.detail: Obil is an officer of King David, responsible for managing the camels of the royal court. His name literally means "camel driver." Although little known, he appears in the list of administrative officials of the kingdom, reflecting the importance of animal husbandry and the complex organization of David's court.
H0179.origine: The name Obil comes from the Semitic root meaning "to lead" or "to guide," hence "one who leads camels." It is a typically Eastern name, borne by an Ishmaelite, that is, a descendant of Ishmael, son of Abraham. Names derived from this root often reflect functions related to herding or guiding animals.
H0179.emploi: Obil is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:30. He appears in a detailed list of David's officers, each responsible for a part of the royal treasury or resources. Obil is specifically designated as "the Ishmaelite," which highlights his foreign origin and perhaps his recognized expertise in camels, valuable and less familiar animals to the Hebrews. His position shows that David, despite his military victories, maintained a vast commercial and agricultural network requiring specialists.
H0179.portee: The mention of Obil reminds us that God's people did not function in isolation: David surrounded himself with individuals from diverse backgrounds, recognizing their skills. It also illustrates the administrative wisdom of a king who understood the importance of good resource management.

sens: important and permanent watercourse flowing to the sea or a low area
watercourse that delineates a region or served as a geographical marker
H0180.detail:
1. A river is a large natural watercourse, larger than a stream, that flows continuously. It is a constant and major body of water in the landscape, capable of serving as a natural boundary or an easily recognizable landmark. In Daniel's vision, the river Ulai is this permanent watercourse near the Persian capital of Susa, where the prophet sees the ram and the goat of his vision (Daniel 8:2, 8:3, 8:6).
2. By extension, a river can serve as a visible marker or boundary in a narrative, landscape, or geography. It marks a specific place and helps the reader or seer to orient themselves. Here, the river Ulai is the anchor point of the vision: it is "near the river" that Daniel sees the symbolic beasts manifest and confront each other.
H0180.origine: The word אוּבַל (uval) designates a significant watercourse. It is attested in Aramaic (the language of this section of Daniel) and would correspond to a perennial watercourse, different from a mere seasonal torrent. The river Ulai mentioned here is a historically real watercourse, the Eulaeus or Choaspes of ancient sources, which flowed near Susa in ancient Persia.
H0180.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Bible, all in chapter 8 of the book of Daniel, and always refers to the same river Ulai. In these three instances, the river serves as a concrete geographical marker to situate the vision that Daniel receives: the ram stands "before the river" (Daniel 8:3), and it is also "near the river" that the vision unfolds (Daniel 8:2). The river remains a fixed element of the visionary setting, marking the place where the action takes place.
H0180.portee: For the reader, this word anchors Daniel's prophetic vision in a concrete geographical reality. Although Daniel is in captivity in Babylon, his vision symbolically transports him to Persia with its real watercourses. This concrete detail—the river Ulai—reinforces the credibility and precision of the revelation: God does not give abstract visions, but images rooted in places and landscapes that human beings know and can visualize.

sens: burning or glowing piece of wood
remnant of a fire that has survived
H0181.detail:
1. An ember is a piece of wood that burns or glows in a fire. It is a coal, a portion of burning wood. Isaiah sees "two ends of smoking embers": the image of kings threatening Judah by shouting fire, but whose fury will extinguish — they are just small flames, not real fires (Isaiah 7:4).
2. By extension, an ember refers to someone or something miraculously escaped from total destruction. Amos reminds Israel that it has been pulled from the fire of ruin, "like a brand plucked from the fire" — God saved it from judgment, but it did not change its heart (Amos 4:11). Similarly, the prophet Zechariah sees Joshua the high priest as "a brand plucked from the fire": Jerusalem narrowly escaped destruction, and God removed it from danger at the last moment (Zechariah 3:2).
H0181.origine: The Hebrew word אוּד (ud) literally means "burning wood." It evokes the remnant of a pyre, the part that is still burning or has burned. The family of the word revolves around the idea of flame and heat. In Greek, this word is often translated as "lemma" or terms evoking fire and flame.
H0181.emploi: This word appears three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, always in a context of threat or salvation. Isaiah uses it to minimize the threat of enemy kings: they are just "smoking brands" destined to extinguish. Amos and Zechariah use it in the opposite sense: it is Israel and Jerusalem that are "brands plucked from the fire," meaning miraculous survivors preserved from total destruction. The word always carries an emotional charge: it speaks of end, judgment, and salvation by the hand of God.
H0181.portee: This word reminds the reader that God controls the fury of our enemies (it lasts no longer than a brand that extinguishes) and that He preserves us from deserved destruction. If we are still here, it is because God has "pulled us from the fire." This inspires both humility and gratitude: we live by a grace that we do not control.

sens: Reason for which an action occurs or a situation exists
Point, question, or event that provokes a dispute or complaint
Motive for anger or reproach towards someone
H0182.detail:
1. The cause is the deep reason that explains why something happens. It is the why of an event or a decision. Abraham is distressed "because of" his son Ishmael (Genesis 21:11), meaning because this word directly concerns and affects him.
2. It is also a subject of conflict or debate: the precise point on which a quarrel or accusation hinges. Abraham addresses reproaches to Abimelech "regarding" a well that his servants have taken by force (Genesis 21:25): this is the sticking point between them.
3. The word finally designates the occasion or motive that provokes an emotional reaction, anger, or judgment. The valley receives its name "because of" the cluster found (Numbers 13:24): this remarkable fact is the occasion for the name given.
H0182.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of giving a reason, explaining, or making known. It is related to the action of speaking about something, accounting for it. The word often appears in narrative formulas where the biblical author introduces a fact or circumstance that justifies what has happened or what will happen.
H0182.emploi: This word appears about ten times in the Old Testament, especially in the historical narratives of Genesis and Exodus. It serves to introduce or explain the reasons for an action, decision, or accusation. Abraham acts "because of" his son, the servants speak "of" the well of water found, a valley receives its name "because of" a remarkable event. In all cases, the word creates a logical link between an event and its consequences or explanations. It can also introduce a subject of reproach or discussion, as when Miriam and Aaron speak "about" the woman that Moses has married.
H0182.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, events are never random or isolated: each has a reason, an origin, a cause. For the reader, this invites us to seek to understand the "why" of things, to connect facts together, and to recognize the hand of God acting according to wise reasons. It also reinforces the awareness that our words and actions have motives and visible consequences.

sens: To feel a strong longing, an attraction towards something or someone
To covet, to seek to possess what belongs to another
To yearn for, to intensely aspire to
To be greedy, to have a craving for food or drink
To attach oneself to someone, to wish for their presence or friendship
H0183.detail:
1. The verb expresses a vivid and intense desire, an inclination of the whole soul towards an object: in Deuteronomy 14:26, the Israelite buys with his money "whatever you desire," meaning everything that truly attracts his heart, everything he ardently wishes.
2. Desire can become wrong when it turns towards what does not belong to us or is not suitable for us: "Do not desire to be with them," says Proverbs 24:1 about the wicked, for coveting their friendship or company leads to sin.
3. This desire is often a longing, a deep aspiration: in 2 Samuel 23:15, David longs for water from the well of Bethlehem, he has an intense craving that torments him.
4. The word particularly applies to greed and bodily appetites: in Numbers 11:4, the "mixed multitude" is "seized with craving" for meat, showing a carnal and insatiable desire.
5. It can describe an inclination of the heart towards a person or a project: "your soul will desire" in 1 Kings 11:37 means that the heart aspires to accomplish, to possess, to experience something.
H0183.origine: The Hebrew verb אָוָה is a primitive root that fundamentally expresses the idea of leaning towards, reaching after. It is a movement of desire, an inclination of the whole soul. The family of the word includes covetousness and envy, often in a passionate or even carnal sense. The word appears mainly in wisdom and narrative texts to explore the hidden movements of the human heart.
H0183.emploi: The verb appears 26 times in the Old Testament. It is found primarily in historical narratives (Numbers, Samuel, Kings), the Psalms, and especially in Proverbs and Ecclesiastes, where wisdom explores the appetites of the heart. Its meaning oscillates between legitimate desire (that of a shepherd who thirsts for fresh water) and reprehensible desire (the covetousness of evil, greed). In Deuteronomy, it describes the people's right to enjoy God's blessings; in Proverbs, it warns against appetites that corrupt the soul. Contexts show that it is the *object* of desire that determines its goodness or malice.
H0183.portee: This word speaks to the reader about the reality of desire: it should neither be denied nor cursed, but discerned and directed. The Christian recognizes that God Himself creates in us legitimate desires, but that the natural heart also tends towards what corrupts and destroys. It is an invitation to examine what truly attracts our soul and to ask God that our desires align with His will and holiness.

sens: mark a boundary by drawing a line
define a territory with boundaries or marks
H0184.detail:
1. To trace a limit or boundary by marking the ground: this is the action of drawing a line that separates two areas. In Numbers 34:10, God commands the people of Israel to trace the eastern boundary of the Promised Land, from Hazar-enan to Shepham — a precise line that would define the territory received as an inheritance.
2. To delimit a territory by marking it so that everyone knows their own boundaries: this transforms a region into a defined and recognizable domain. The action implies that the boundary should be visible and stable, so that no one is in doubt about what belongs to whom.
H0184.origine: The Hebrew verb אָוָה (avah) literally means "to mark" or "to draw a mark." It is related to the idea of making a visible trace, leaving an imprint. In its reflexive form (Hithpael), the verb takes on the meaning of "to measure oneself" or "to mark oneself" — that is, to assign oneself a limit or to define oneself in relation to boundaries.
H0184.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible (Numbers 34:10), in the context where God prescribes to the people of Israel how to delimit the borders of the Promised Land. It is a technical term for measurement and territorial delimitation, used to indicate a concrete and official action. Its unique usage makes it a rare word, but very clear in its function: it is about physically marking a line that will be the boundary.
H0184.portee: This word reminds us that God's will for His people is clear and precise: God does not give vague and undefined lands, but assigns certain limits. For the reader, this shows that divine order often comes with practical and measurable details — God does not speak in riddles when it comes to the promised inheritance. Tracing the boundaries also acknowledges that each part has its limits, and that receiving an inheritance means accepting boundaries.

sens: Desire, will for something
Passionate inclination, often physical
Natural appetite or need
H0185.detail:
1. Desire is a simple and legitimate longing for something: the will to accomplish an action or obtain a good. In Deuteronomy 12:20, the people of Israel may kill livestock and eat meat "according to the desire" of their heart, meaning simply because they want to — it is neither forbidden nor shameful.
2. Desire can be a passionate inclination, sometimes intense or carnal, that drives one to act. Jeremiah 2:24 illustrates this by describing a wild donkey "panting in the heat of its passion," seeking to satisfy its natural desire. Here, the word denotes a visceral inclination.
3. Desire can express a deep will or a wish of the heart. In 1 Samuel 23:20, the Ziphites tell King Saul that it is "all the desire of your soul" — they mean that it is what he truly wants, his dearest wish.
H0185.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of wanting, coveting, reaching for something. It has no intrinsic moral connotation: desire is neither good nor bad in itself — it all depends on its object. The root appears in other forms to mean "to sigh after," "to covet," or "to wish." In the Hebrew Bible, a distinction is made between natural and legitimate desire (to be hungry, to want something) and guilty desire (to covet another's goods).
H0185.emploi: This word appears 7 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the historical and prophetic books. It is particularly frequent in Deuteronomy, where it speaks of the desire to eat, the Levite's will to go to the sanctuary (Deuteronomy 18:6), or simply an act done according to one's own will. In 1 Samuel 23:20, it denotes the king Saul's most secret wish. In Jeremiah 2:24, it takes on a passionate and even carnal hue. The word thus applies to both simple needs and the deep longings of the heart, even to animal or sinful inclinations.
H0185.portee: This word invites the Christian reader to reflect on the nature of desire: not all our desires are sins. To be hungry, to want good, to aspire to serve God — these are legitimate desires. The Bible acknowledges that humans naturally desire. But it also warns us that unchecked desire can lead us astray (like the wild donkey) or divert us from justice. Understanding this word helps us discern between what is an innocent need and what becomes a dangerous covetousness.

sens: Father of Palal, one of the rebuilders of the walls of Jerusalem during the Exile and Return
H0186.detail: Uzaï is a Jewish man mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when Nehemiah organizes the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem after the return from exile. His son Palal participates in this work by repairing a section of the walls near the angle and the upper tower of the royal palace, by the prison courtyard (Nehemiah 3:25). Although Uzaï himself is not named as a worker, his mention shows that he was the father of a man active in this great collective restoration effort.
H0186.origine: The name Uzaï literally means "I will be sprinkled" or "My sprinklings," deriving from the Hebrew root that evokes the action of pouring or sprinkling water. It is a theophoric name, formed according to the Jewish conventions of the time, expressing a relationship with God or an expected blessing.
H0186.emploi: Uzaï appears only once in the biblical writings, in Nehemiah 3:25. He is presented as the father of Palal, who is among the many workers and leaders cited in chapter 3 of the book of Nehemiah. This chapter lists all those who participated in the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem around the middle of the fifth century B.C., after the return from exile in Babylon. The mention of Uzaï testifies to the commitment of entire families to this collective restoration project of the capital.

sens: Son of Joktan, listed among the descendants of Shem
H0187G.detail: 1. Uzal is a son of Joktan, himself a son of Eber (Genesis 10:27). He appears in the genealogy of the peoples descended from Shem, at the origins of humanity after the Flood. His name appears in the list of the twelve sons of Joktan, alongside figures like Sheba, Ophir, and Havilah, some of whom will give their name to regions or peoples. The same genealogy is repeated in 1 Chronicles 1:21, confirming his stable place in the biblical genealogical tradition.
H0187G.origine: The name Uzal means "I will be flooded," according to etymological tradition. Like many names of the descendants of Shem in Genesis 10, it likely designates an eponymous ancestor, that is, the founder or legendary ancestor of a people or region. These names often reflect places or peoples of the ancient Near East known to the biblical writers.
H0187G.emploi: Uzal is mentioned exactly twice in the Bible: in Genesis 10:27 and in 1 Chronicles 1:21, which repeat the same genealogy. He is a purely genealogical figure, without any narrative of action. His name is part of the list of the descendants of Joktan, son of Eber, and represents a link in the genealogical chain that connects Noah to the peoples of the earth after the Flood. This repetition in two books underscores the importance that biblical tradition places on these genealogies.

sens: Son of Joktan
Region or trading people in ancient Arabia
H0187H.detail: 1. Uzal is the sixth son of Joktan, himself the son of Eber, in the genealogy of the Semitic peoples after the Flood (Genesis 10). He represents one of the branches of Abraham's family. 2. Uzal also refers to a region or people of ancient Arabia known for its prosperous trade: Ezekiel 27:19 mentions it among the suppliers of Tyre, alongside Vedan and Javan, offering worked iron, cassia (cinnamon), and aromatic reed — precious products of ancient Middle Eastern trade.
H0187H.origine: The name Uzal literally means "I will be flooded" or "abundant flow" in Hebrew, perhaps evoking a fertile territory or a port site. The name refers to the descendants of Joktan and, through them, to the population of the southern Arabian regions and the Persian Gulf. Most of Joktan's sons in Genesis correspond to historically attested peoples or regions in Arabia.
H0187H.emploi: Uzal appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 27:19, in the list of nations that trade with Tyre at the height of its prosperity. This passage inventories the peoples supplying the great Phoenician city: Uzal is listed as an exporter of luxury goods and precious raw materials, confirming its significant economic status in antiquity. The context shows that it was an established and wealthy trading partner.
H0187H.portee: This biblical passage reveals how God, in His sovereignty, arranges nations and their riches. Uzal, a distant and prosperous people, symbolizes the extent of the ancient world's trading network and the pride of earthly powers — Tyre itself, despite its commercial glory, will be judged by God. This reminder teaches us that material wealth and economic power, however considerable they may be in the eyes of men, remain under divine judgment.

sens: Exclamation of pain, desolation, or despair in the face of impending or realized misfortune
Prophetic warning cry announcing God's judgment
Personal lament in the face of suffering or ruin
H0188.detail:
1. It is primarily a passionate exclamation, a cry from the heart torn by fear or pain: "Woe to us!" cries the people when they see the destroyer approaching (Jeremiah 4:13). It expresses terror in the face of disaster, the feeling of being lost.
2. In the mouths of the prophets, it is a solemn warning of God's judgment: "Woe to the wicked! he will be in misfortune" (Isaiah 3:11), or "Woe to you, Moab! You are lost" (Numbers 21:29). The word becomes a word of condemnation.
3. It can also be a personal groan, the lament of someone who suffers: Jeremiah says, "Woe to me! I am broken! My wound is painful!" (Jeremiah 10:19), as if his very existence had become an unbearable burden.
H0188.origine: This Hebrew word is an interjection, a word that escapes rather than a word constructed according to ordinary rules. It expresses raw emotion, the instinctive cry. It is the Hebrew equivalent of our "Alas!" or "Oh no!" in French. The word has no root in the strictly grammatical sense; it is a fixed exclamation by usage, like our "Oh God!".
H0188.emploi: The word appears 23 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah) and the lamentations. In the historical books (1 Samuel, Numbers), it appears in the cries of the people in the face of peril. In prophecy, it is never neutral: it always announces the judgment or ruin of the one to whom it is addressed (Isaiah 3:11, Jeremiah 4:13). Particularly in Jeremiah, it is also the personal lament of the prophet himself, crushed by his message (Jeremiah 10:19, 45:3). It can address a nation (Moab in Numbers 21:29), a class of people (the wicked in Isaiah 3:11), or oneself.
H0188.portee: This interjection reminds us that the Bible does not hide the reality of misfortune and suffering: it gives voice to those who cry under the weight of divine judgment or distress. For the believer, the word "woe" in the mouth of a prophet is a call to repentance, a warning that God takes sin seriously. And when Jeremiah or another groans "Woe to me!", it is a biblical permission to weep over our ruins without pretending that all is well.

sens: Chief of Midian at the time of the Exodus and conquest
H0189.detail: Evi is one of the five chiefs or kings of Midian mentioned in the Bible. He first appears in Numbers 31:8, where Moses orders the Israelites to fight against the Midianites in retaliation for having seduced them into idolatry. Evi is killed during this battle, alongside four other Midianite chiefs: Rekem, Zur, Hur, and Reba. Later, in Joshua 13:21, the same list is repeated to describe the territories that Moses had conquered east of the Jordan: Evi is referred to there as a "prince" or "chief" who was under Sihon, the king of the Amorites, and who lived in the land.
H0189.origine: The name Evi, according to tradition, means "my desire." It is a Midianite name, typical of the desert peoples of Arabia with whom Israel had contact during the patriarchal and Mosaic periods.
H0189.emploi: Evi appears in two key passages of the Old Testament, both in the context of the conquest of lands east of the Jordan. In Numbers 31, he dies during Israel's campaign against Midian, ordered by Moses to punish the Midianites who had led the people astray. In Joshua 13, his name reappears as an illustration of the defeated chiefs whose territories were distributed to the tribes of Israel. He is a historical figure of secondary importance, mentioned only to document the conquest.

sens: Exclamation of lament or mourning
H0190.detail: 1. It is an interjection, that is, a spontaneous cry of affliction. It expresses misfortune, pain, or regret in the face of a difficult situation. In Psalm 120:5, the psalmist cries out: "Woe is me that I dwell in Meshech!" — he laments his captivity and exile far from home.
H0190.origine: The word comes from a root expressing pain or misfortune. It is a short, intense interjection, like those uttered by someone in distress: it captures the natural cry of one who suffers.
H0190.emploi: This interjection appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 120:5, where it opens a psalm of lamentation. The psalmist uses it to express his dismay at his prolonged stay away from his land and people. It sets the tone for the entire psalm: that of a sincere lament, of a soul wounded by exile.
H0190.portee: This exclamation teaches us that it is right to cry out our pain before God. The psalmist does not hide his misfortune or suffering: he expresses them freely in prayer. It is an invitation to honesty before God, not to stifle our groans but to entrust them to the One who listens.

sens: One who lacks wisdom and discernment
One who acts without considering the consequences
One who despises instruction and the fear of God
One who provokes quarrels and conflicts through their words
One who behaves without restraint or moral control
H0191.detail:
1. The fool is primarily one who lacks practical wisdom for living well. It is a deficiency of moral and spiritual intelligence, not mere brute stupidity. In Proverbs 1:7, we learn that "fools despise wisdom and instruction" — they actively reject what could teach them.
2. The fool acts impulsively, without measuring the dangers. Proverbs 7:22 compares him to "an ox going to the slaughter" — he rushes headlong, unable to foresee the calamity that awaits him.
3. The fool despises the fear of God. He thinks he knows better than God, contesting the established order. In Proverbs 14:9, fools "mock at sin."
4. The fool constantly provokes: his words come out unchecked, creating conflicts. Proverbs 14:3 says, "in the mouth of the fool is a rod for his pride" — he strikes himself with his thoughtless words.
5. The fool lives without self-control, given over to his passions and impulses. In Proverbs 27:22, even if crushed in a mortar, "his folly would not depart from him": his entire nature is corrupted.
H0191.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "lack of sense, lack of discernment." The fool is not one who cannot understand, but one who does not want to — he closes his heart to wisdom. In Hebrew biblical thought, wisdom is not primarily an intellectual ability: it is an attitude of the heart towards God, an obedience and reverential fear. The fool is its exact opposite.
H0191.emploi: The word appears 26 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in Proverbs (17 times) and Psalms. It paints the portrait of moral and spiritual folly. Its characteristic traits: he talks too much (Proverbs 10:14), gets angry easily (Job 5:2), rejects advice (Proverbs 12:15), quarrels for nothing (Proverbs 20:3), despises his parents (Proverbs 15:5). The folly he suffers from is incurable by education alone; it stems from a refusal of the heart. In Jeremiah 4:22, God says of his unfaithful people: "My people is foolish, they do not know me" — a striking equation between fool and one who turns away from God.
H0191.portee: For the Christian, this word is a call to introspection: true folly is not lacking intelligence, but rejecting the wisdom of God. It invites us to cultivate a humble attitude towards the Word, to allow ourselves to be taught rather than following our own judgment. It is also a warning: folly has visible consequences — anger, conflicts, destruction — while wisdom produces peace and life.

sens: King of Babylon, son and successor of Nebuchadnezzar
H0192.detail: Evil-Merodach is the king who ruled over the Neo-Babylonian empire after the death of Nebuchadnezzar, from 562 to 560 BC. His name means "man of Merodach," Merodach being the chief god of the Babylonians. The Bible mentions him for a remarkable act of mercy: he released Jehoiachin, the king of Judah, from his prison in Babylon (2 Kings 25:27).
H0192.origine: The name "Evil-Merodach" combines two elements: "Evil" or "Awil," which means "man" in Akkadian, and "Merodach," the name of the chief Babylonian god. It is a royal Akkadian name that indicates his connection to the deity worshiped in Babylon. Babylonian records confirm that he was the son and immediate successor of Nebuchadnezzar II.
H0192.emploi: Evil-Merodach appears twice in the Bible, in two parallel passages: 2 Kings 25:27 and Jeremiah 52:31. In both cases, he is presented at the moment he ascends to the throne of Babylon. The Bible reports a unique event from his reign: the thirty-seventh year after Jehoiachin was imprisoned, the Babylonian king released the Judean king from prison, honored him, and granted him a privileged place at his court. This act of grace towards a defeated king is the only remarkable fact attributed to this king in the biblical texts.
H0192.portee: The account of Evil-Merodach releasing Jehoiachin from prison shows that even in the midst of exile and defeat, God has not completely abandoned his people. This unexpected mercy from a foreign king towards a captive king reminds us that God can use those who know him little to accomplish his goodness towards his own. It is a sign of hope amid the darkest pages of Judah's history.

sens: The belly, the trunk of the human body
Physical strength and vitality embodied in the body
The fleshly appearance of a person, especially their corpulence
H0193A.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the physical body, particularly the belly and abdomen. In Psalms 73:4, it describes the wicked whose "body is laden with fat": the psalmist speaks of these prosperous men who seem to enjoy an easy life, and whose well-fed bodies testify to the material abundance they enjoy.
2. By extension, the body represents physical strength and vitality. Having a robust, healthy body means enjoying health and material prosperity.
3. In a figurative and slightly derogatory sense, it can evoke carnal materiality, particularly when it is excessive or becomes a subject of reproach: the psalmist highlights this ironic contrast between the bodily serenity of the wicked and the torments of the righteous.
H0193A.origine: The Hebrew root אול (ul) evokes the idea of prominence, of what rises or bulges. The word emphasizes the visible and carnal aspect of the body, particularly its mass and volume. It is a rather concrete and direct term, which can take on a derogatory tone depending on the context, especially when it comes to criticizing bodily or material excess.
H0193A.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Psalms 73:4. It describes the fleshy and well-fed body of the prosperous wicked, in a passage where the psalmist contemplates the apparent injustice of the world: the ungodly seem to prosper without suffering, their bodies testifying to their material ease. The context is one of meditation on divine providence and the mystery of the suffering of the righteous in the face of the wicked.
H0193A.portee: This word invites the believer not to envy the physical and material prosperity of the wicked. A well-fed body is not proof of divine blessing, and carnal ease does not bring happiness to one who is separated from God. It is a call to look beyond appearances and material goods to seek true wealth: communion with the Lord.

sens: expresses a possibility, an uncertainty about what will happen
expresses a wish, a hope that something is true or will come to pass
expresses a supposition, a hypothetical condition
expresses a doubt about what exists or has happened
H0194.detail:
1. The word marks uncertainty about the future: one does not know if something will happen or not. Sarai says to Abram: "Perhaps I shall have children by her" (Genesis 16:2), as she does not know if this plan will work. It expresses an open possibility, without certainty.
2. The word expresses hope that a prayer will be answered or that an action will bear fruit. Jeremiah pleads: "Perhaps the Lord will hear their supplications" (Jeremiah 36:7), maintaining hope even without guarantee. Jonathan also says: "Perhaps the Lord will act for us" (1 Samuel 14:6), expressing a confidence mixed with uncertainty.
3. The word serves to evoke a hypothesis to explore its consequences: "Perhaps the woman will not want to follow me" (Genesis 24:5), the servant considers a possible scenario. It poses a condition to reflect on what one would do then.
4. The word can also express a slight doubt about what is true, when one asks someone to verify: "Perhaps you have sinned?" suggests the idea that this may have happened, without asserting it.
H0194.origine: This Hebrew word fundamentally expresses uncertainty, the unfixed nature of what has not yet happened. It comes from a root that marks the idea of "in case" or "if by chance." In Hebrew, it is an adverb of modality that shades the sentence with a conditional or dubitative nuance. Unlike words that affirm or deny with certainty, this one suspends judgment and opens the door to multiple possibilities.
H0194.emploi: This word appears 44 times in the Old Testament, very often in the language of prayer and supplication. It is found at crucial moments when biblical characters ask God to accomplish something but recognize that they cannot force it: Job prays "perhaps" that his sons have offended God (Job 1:5), Jeremiah hopes "perhaps" that the people will repent (Jeremiah 36:7). It is also seen in careful planning: Abraham's servant considers "perhaps" that the woman will refuse to follow him (Genesis 24:5). Sometimes it expresses a timid confidence in the face of the impossible: Jonathan and his young man go into battle "perhaps" the Lord will save them (1 Samuel 14:6). It is the word of the believer who trusts God while recognizing that he does not control the outcome.
H0194.portee: This word teaches us humility: even when we pray or hope, we are never certain of the outcome, for our lives depend on God. It also reveals authentic faith, one that acts and prays without demanding a guarantee. Jonathan charges into battle "perhaps" the Lord will act — his trust does not paralyze his action, it inspires it. The word invites the reader to distinguish between caution (recognizing possibilities) and fear (refusing to act).

sens: river in the region of Elam, in ancient Persia
H0195.detail: 1. The river Ulaï is a watercourse that flows through the province of Elam, a historical region in southwestern Persia (modern-day Iran). In Daniel's vision, the prophet sees himself placed "by the river Ulaï" in Susa, the capital of Elam (Daniel 8:2), and it is "in the midst of the Ulaï" that he hears a human voice commanding Gabriel to explain the vision (Daniel 8:16). The river thus serves as a geographical landmark within the supernatural context of the apocalyptic vision.
H0195.origine: The name Ulaï means "my leaders" or "my mighty ones" in Hebrew, formed from the root denoting strength or power. It is the proper name of a real river in Elam, which has retained this name throughout ancient history. This river, also known by other ancient names, marked the political and religious geography of the Persian world contemporary to Daniel.
H0195.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, exclusively in chapter 8 of the book of Daniel, which reports the prophet's apocalyptic vision concerning future empires. Daniel receives this vision in the specific context of the city of Susa, near the river Ulaï: this geographical detail anchors the supernatural vision in a real and known space, Elam being a major historical power. The river becomes the setting where the prophet hears the divine command, establishing a link between the visible world and the celestial realm.

sens: Who acts or speaks without good sense
Who lacks wisdom and discernment
Who is devoid of practical reason
H0196.detail: 1. The fool is one who acts without considering the consequences, without judging reality soundly. In Zechariah 11:15, God commands the prophet to take "the equipment of a foolish shepherd," meaning the tools and style of a shepherd who poorly governs his flock, who does not understand or ignores what his responsibilities require. 2. It is a moral and practical folly: not a disease of the mind, but a choice or habit of living without listening to God's word and the wisdom He offers. The fool refuses to learn and change course.
H0196.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the absence or loss of common sense. It designates one who does not think, who does not use his intelligence to discern good from evil, the wise from the fool. This term belongs to the biblical vocabulary of wisdom and discernment, where the fool is the opposite of the wise.
H0196.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Zechariah 11:15, where it qualifies the style of a false shepherd. God asks Zechariah to don this "foolish" equipment to figuratively and ironically depict the bad shepherd who opposes God and does not care for the flock according to divine will. It is a word of wisdom: the fool is one who refuses to listen to God.
H0196.portee: Recognizing the fool within oneself and in false teachers helps the believer discern who truly deserves his listening and trust. The fear of God and the love of wisdom protect us from this spiritual insensitivity that characterizes one who ignores or rejects God's word.

sens: Covered gallery supported by columns
Entrance or vestibule of a prestigious building
Architectural space of prestige and reception
H0197G.detail:
1. A portico is a covered gallery or hall whose roof is supported by aligned columns or pillars. In Solomon's palace, the portico of the columns measures fifty cubits long and thirty cubits wide (1 Kings 7:6), which shows the scale and magnificence of this construction.
2. It is also an entry or transition space, like an impressive vestibule. In 1 Kings 7:8, Solomon has his dwelling built "behind the portico," suggesting that the portico is a reception area before accessing the private apartments.
3. The portico has a function of prestige and display: it is a space that showcases the power and wealth of the king. The mention of a portico for Pharaoh's daughter (1 Kings 7:8) and the comparison with the portico of the Temple (1 Kings 7:12) highlight its architectural and symbolic importance.
H0197G.origine: The Hebrew word ʾulâm designates a specific architectural structure, probably a covered space framed by columns. The biblical context shows it linked to the grand palatial and religious constructions of the ancient Near East. It is a characteristic element of royal and sacred architecture during Solomon's time.
H0197G.emploi: The word appears three times, exclusively in the account of Solomon's constructions in 1 Kings 7. It first describes the "portico of the columns" of the royal palace (verse 6), then the portico as a major architectural element of the king's residence (verse 8), and finally is used to describe the portico of the Temple itself (verse 12). These uses show that the portico is a standard element of the grand prestigious buildings of the ancient Near East, both a major circulation space and a symbol of magnificence.
H0197G.portee: This word reminds us that the splendor of human constructions, even royal ones, was organized according to a particular and functional architecture. It testifies to Solomon's wisdom in managing resources and organizing space. For the believer, the implicit parallel between the royal palace and the Temple underscores that God's house deserved equal attention to that of the king.

sens: Covered construction supported by columns, forming the entrance of a building
Open but protected space, serving as a passage or waiting area
In Solomon's palace, the hall where the king rendered justice
H0197H.detail:
1. A portico is an architectural construction formed by a roof supported by columns or pillars, which extends the entrance of a large building and protects it. It serves as a transitional space between the outside and the inside.

2. More broadly, it is a covered gallery but open on the sides, which can serve as a passage or gathering place. It offers the shelter of a roof without completely enclosing the space.

3. In Solomon's palace, this portico was specifically intended for justice: the king held his throne there and rendered his judgments as the supreme judge of Israel. It was thus a place of authority and royal decision (1 Kings 7:7).
H0197H.origine: The Hebrew word אוּלָם (ulam) designates a hall or covered space. Its etymology evokes the idea of a distinct, separate place, possibly related to isolation or delimitation. This word appears in the architectural descriptions of the temple and palaces of ancient Israel, where it designates the ante-rooms or covered halls, that is, spaces of structural and functional importance.
H0197H.emploi: The word appears only once in the provided Bible (1 Kings 7:7), but it designates a major element of Solomon's palace architecture. In this context, the portico of judgment is not just a passage: it is the official hall where the king of Judah exercises his role as judge and final arbiter. It is built of cedar, a noble and durable material, thus affirming the importance and permanence of royal justice. This portico illustrates how Solomon materially organizes the exercise of judicial power in Israel.
H0197H.portee: This portico reminds us that in the Bible, justice is not an abstraction, but is embodied in places and people. Solomon's judgment hall becomes a symbol of royal authority put at the service of equity. For the believer, this evokes the idea that God Himself judges with justice, and that His judgments are exercised with majesty and clarity.

sens: Covered construction forming an entrance or open passage, with columns or a roof
H0197I.detail: 1. The portico is a covered architectural structure, generally with columns, that serves as a protected passage or entrance. In Solomon's temple, it was not just a simple roof, but a noble space where the king rendered justice. In 1 Kings 7:7, Solomon had a throne portico built where he sat to judge; this space was covered with precious cedar "from the floor to the ceiling," highlighting its importance and splendor.
H0197I.origine: The Hebrew word אוּלָם (ulam) designates a hall or covered vestibule. It appears in architectural contexts, particularly for the constructions of the temple. Its precise etymology remains debated, but the word is regularly used for covered and important spaces of the sanctuary.
H0197I.emploi: The word appears only once in the provided Segond translations: in 1 Kings 7:7, describing the arrangements of Solomon's royal palace. It specifically designates the throne portico, the place where royal justice was exercised. This usage emphasizes that the portico is not just a simple shelter, but a space of power and dignity adorned with precious materials.
H0197I.portee: This portico recalls the majesty of Solomon's reign and illustrates how architecture serves to reflect power and authority. For the believer, this evokes how order, beauty, and justice must be linked: the place where justice is rendered is a space of splendor.

sens: Covered entrance or gallery preceding a building, particularly the temple
Space delimited by columns or posts at the front of a construction
Passage or threshold by which one accesses a sacred place
H0197J.detail:
1. The portico is the covered entrance space that precedes the temple or one of its dependencies. In 1 Kings 6:3, the portico in front of the temple measures twenty cubits in length and ten in depth: it is a clearly defined architectural structure, serving as an interface between the outside and the inside of the sanctuary.

2. The term also designates the structure itself, delimited by posts or columns. Ezekiel 40:9 specifies its exact dimensions: the vestibule of the gate measures eight cubits, with posts of two cubits; it is a measurable and constructed architectural element.

3. The portico functions as a spiritual and practical threshold: in Ezekiel 44:3, the prince enters there to sit and eat bread before the Lord. In 2 Chronicles 29:17, the priests enter the portico of the Lord to purify the temple, marking the beginning of sacred work.
H0197J.origine: The Hebrew word אוּלָם (ulam) properly designates an entry room or vestibule. Its root evokes the idea of a prominent or enclosed structure. The term mainly appears in the descriptions of Solomon's temple and the vision of Ezekiel's temple, where it plays an important structural and symbolic role in sacred architecture.
H0197J.emploi: This word appears 25 times in the Old Testament, concentrated in two contexts: first in the description of Solomon's temple and its extensions (1 Kings 6-7; 2 Chronicles 3, 8, 15, 29), and then massively in the detailed visions of the temple prophesied by Ezekiel (40 chapters). The portico is always a measured element described with precision, marking a structural access point. Its dimensions and materials (pure gold covering in 2 Chronicles 3:4) reflect the importance of the building. In Joel 2:17, the priests weep between the portico and the altar, showing that it is a place of intercession.
H0197J.portee: The portico reminds us that access to God is not improvised: it goes through steps, thresholds, and progression. It is both an invitation and a barrier, marking that the approach to the divine requires respect and intention. For the Christian, this evokes that our communion with God, although opened by Jesus Christ, calls for an awareness of the sacred nature of this relationship.

sens: Man from the tribe of Manasseh during the divided monarchy
Member of Saul's royal family among the Benjamites
H0198G.detail:
1. Ulam is a man of Manasseh, son of Sheresh and brother of Rekem (1 Chronicles 7:16). He is the father of Bedan and belongs to the genealogy of the descendants of Gilead, son of Machir (1 Chronicles 7:17). He is a minor character in Israel's history, known only by his place in this tribal lineage.

2. Another Ulam belonged to Saul's family among the Benjamites. Although few details are given, his presence in the royal genealogies shows his genealogical importance within the chosen people.
H0198G.origine: The name Ulam means "their chief" or "vestibule." It is a Hebrew personal name used to designate specific men in the genealogies of Israel. Two distinct men bear this name in Chronicles, one Manassite and the other Benjamite.
H0198G.emploi: Ulam appears twice in the Bible, both in 1 Chronicles 7. First mentioned in verse 16 as the son of Sheresh and brother of Rekem in the Manassite genealogy, he is then named in verse 17 as the father of Bedan. These two verses constitute the entirety of the biblical information about this character. He is an important link in the tribal genealogies of Israel, serving to establish the continuity of lineages after the division of the kingdom.

sens: Benjamite of the royal family of Saul
Leader or ancestor of a warrior branch of Benjamin
H0198H.detail:
1. Ulam was a man from the tribe of Benjamin, living during the time of the divided monarchy. He was the son of Elah and the brother of Jeush and Eliphelet, as indicated in 1 Chronicles 8:39.
2. His descendants are presented as valiant men, archers, who had many sons and grandsons — one hundred fifty in total according to 1 Chronicles 8:40. This suggests that Ulam was the leader of an important and combative branch of the royal family of Saul.
H0198H.origine: The name Ulam means "their chief" or "vestibule," which may reflect a role of protection or leadership within his family. It is a typical Hebrew name in the familial and political context of the kingdoms of Israel and Judah.
H0198H.emploi: Ulam appears only twice in the Bible, both in 1 Chronicles 8:39-40, in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin and the house of Saul. He is mentioned as the firstborn of Elah, and the emphasis is placed on his warrior lineage: his sons and grandsons are described as strong and skilled archers, forming a clan of one hundred fifty people. His importance lies less in himself than in his warrior lineage.
H0198H.portee: Ulam reminds the reader that the strength of Israel rested on united and valiant family clans. His numerous warrior descendants show how, in the political and military order of Israel, families perpetuated themselves and remained sources of power. It is also a testimony to God's faithfulness to the tribe of Benjamin, despite the divisions that ran through the people.

sens: Marks a strong opposition or restriction between two thoughts
Introduces a correction or nuance to what has just been said
Expresses a contrast: one of the two things is true, the other is not
Serves to introduce an important statement that contradicts or surpasses what precedes
H0199.detail: 1. This word connects two ideas by showing that they oppose or contradict each other. It says "not this, but this" emphatically. For example, in Genesis 28:19, we learn that Jacob names a place Bethel, "but" the city had previously another name, Luz — the two names oppose each other. 2. Sometimes it nuances rather than opposes: it tempers what has just been said, as in 1 Samuel 25:34, where David acknowledges that Nabal has offended him, "but" God has restrained him from taking revenge. The "but" adds a new perspective. 3. Very often, this word prepares a crucial statement. In Job 13:3, Job says he does not want to argue with his friends, "but" he wants to speak directly to God — the "but" marks a turning point, the real subject. 4. H0199.origine: This Hebrew word comes from an ancient root meaning "really" or "certainly." It has specialized to mark opposition. It belongs to the family of words that reinforce or contrast: this is why the translation "but" fits very well — this "but" is not weak as in modern French, it is a "but" that insists, that says "really, on the contrary."
H0199.emploi: This word appears 19 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is mostly found in the narratives of Genesis and Exodus, where it corrects names or genealogies (Genesis 28:19; Judges 18:29), and very frequently in the book of Job, where it serves to express objections, corrections, and Job's passionate appeals to God in the face of his friends' theology (Job 1:11, 13:3, 13:4, 14:18, 17:10, 33:1). In 1 Samuel 25:34, it introduces God's decisive intervention. Everywhere, it is a strong conjunction of contrast, never a simple logical link.
H0199.portee: This small word shows us how the Bible breathes through contrasts. When God or a character says "but," we must listen: this is where the meaning changes. Job resorts to this "but" to cry out his conviction despite doubt; this is also how God announces His turnarounds. For the Christian, recognizing these "buts" in biblical reading is learning to hear where God truly places His emphasis, where the story changes direction.
